Where’s Yours?

Aunt Bev was buried on the Tuesday before Thanksgiving in 2023. By Sunday the casseroles were gone, the folding chairs were back in the church basement, and Jess was sitting at my kitchen table with her coat still on, holding an envelope from the county probate court.

It was addressed to me. Bev had named me her executor.

Jess turned the envelope over twice. She teaches seventh-grade science in Columbus, and she has a teacher’s way of asking a question she already knows the answer to.

“Mom,” she said. “Where’s yours?”

I had an answer for every question about Bev that week. Which bank. Which drawer. Which cousin had the key to the storage unit. I did not have an answer for that one.

Here’s the truth, and I’ll give it to you the way I gave it to myself that afternoon. I had settled my father’s estate and my mother’s since 2016, and Bev’s was just getting started. The newest will in our house was dated 1996. It sat in a manila envelope in the cedar chest at the foot of our bed, under the Christmas tablecloth. It named my parents as Jess’s guardians. Both of my parents were dead, and Jess was thirty-one.

Dale and I had no powers of attorney. No health care papers. No real idea, if I’m honest, who was listed as beneficiary on half our accounts.

Dale was standing in the doorway, drying a coffee mug. “She’s got you there,” he said.

Dale says about one sentence per crisis, and it’s usually the right one.

This book is what happened next: the roughly six months it took the two of us to get from that envelope to signing day in May 2024, and the first yearly review after that. I took notes as we went, because I wanted Jess to have the map, and because I suspected we weren’t the only couple with a 1996 will under a tablecloth.

Who’s talking to you

My name is Ruth Calloway. I’m 61, and I live in a brick ranch on the edge of Chillicothe, Ohio, twenty minutes from the farmhouse I grew up in. For 27 years I kept the books for Dale’s heating-and-cooling business, which means I know what a filing deadline feels like and I own more three-ring binders than anyone should.

I am not a lawyer, an accountant or a financial planner. I’m a daughter, a niece and a bookkeeper who learned this at kitchen tables, from three estates and a lot of hold music. My mother was a paralegal at a law office downtown, so I grew up hearing the word “intestate” over supper without knowing what it meant. Knowing the word didn’t help me much later. Knowing what to do would have.

What I do know is what it costs a family when the papers aren’t there. Mostly not money. Saturdays. Phone calls to people who need a form you don’t have. The slow, particular misery of learning that something could have been fixed with one signature, by a person who can no longer sign.

You’ll hear about Bev’s savings account in Chapter 3. It still makes my jaw tight.

What’s in here, and what isn’t

People are told to “get their affairs in order.” Nobody tells them what the order is. I think that’s the most useless advice in this whole business, and it’s why so many of us own a folder marked IMPORTANT with nothing inside it.

So here is the order this book uses. You make the list first, and you sign last.

Chapter 1 covers what an estate plan actually is and what your state does if you never make one. Chapter 2 is the list. Then come the forms that quietly beat your will, the will itself, guardians for children, and the honest question of whether you need a living trust. After that, the two powers of attorney — one for money, one for your medical care — which do their work while you’re still alive. Then passwords and phones. Then the families that aren’t simple: second marriages, stepchildren, single people, a child who needs extra protection. Chapter 11 is about hiring a lawyer and walking in prepared. Chapter 12 is where to keep it all and how to look at it once a year. By the end you’ll have a one-page review checklist, the same one Dale and I pull out every March.

Each chapter ends with something to do: a sheet to fill in, a script for a hard conversation, or a rule for making a decision. Use them. They’re the part that turns reading into a plan.

Two things this book leaves out on purpose. If you’ve been named someone’s executor and need to know how to do the job, that’s The Executor’s Step-by-Step Guide. If a parent has just died and you’re facing the first weeks, set this book aside and pick up The First 90 Days After a Parent Dies. This one is strictly about your own plan, made while you’re alive and thinking straight.

The honest limits

Most of estate law is state law. The rules on witnesses, on a spouse’s rights, on what happens without a will, on what makes a health care form valid — they differ among Ohio, Arizona, and Pennsylvania, and they change. When a rule varies, I’ll say so and tell you how to check yours. When I use a number, I’ll give its year and where it came from.

The facts in these pages come from places you can look up yourself: the IRS, the National Institute on Aging, the American Bar Association’s estate planning pages, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, and state court self-help centers. My stories come from my family. The rules don’t.

This is general information, not legal advice, and I’d rather show you what that means than repeat it at the bottom of every page. Where you need a lawyer, I’ll tell you plainly, and I’ll tell you why. Minor children, a blended family, property in two states, a business, an heir you mean to leave out, a relative likely to argue — those are lawyer territory. Where you probably can do something yourself, I’ll say that too. Either way, a lawyer is worth a great deal more when you walk in with your homework done. I learned that from Sam, the lawyer in town who handled Bev’s estate and later drew up ours. You’ll meet him.

What no book can do is sign for you.

How to use this book

One chapter per sitting. That’s roughly the pace Dale and I kept, on weeknights after supper, and it’s the pace I’d recommend to anyone with a job and a life. You’ll be tempted to read the whole thing in a weekend and then do nothing. I know, because that’s how I’ve read most books about money.

Keep a pencil nearby. Write on the sheets. Cross things out.

And give the papers a home. Ours is a green accordion file in the second kitchen drawer, the one under the silverware. I bought it at the drugstore the Monday after Jess asked her question, and that night I moved the 1996 will out of the cedar chest and into the first pocket. It was the only thing in there. By May the elastic band was straining. Every sheet in this book went into that file, and nothing came out to live anywhere else.

One more thing before you start. Some of what follows is about your own death, and about a stretch of time when you might not be able to speak for yourself. A few evenings will sit heavy. I won’t pretend otherwise.

But I have sat on the other side of this, with my father’s checkbook and my mother’s shoebox, and I would much rather you did the hard part now, on purpose, than leave it for someone you love to do later in a hurry. That’s what Jess was really asking. It wasn’t morbid. She’d watched me do this for her grandpa, then her grandma, then Bev, and she wanted to know whether she’d be the one at the table next.

She will be, someday. The difference is whether there’s anything on the table when she gets there.

Tonight’s ten minutes

Before you open Chapter 1, take one sheet of paper. Not a notebook, not an app on your phone. One sheet. Write three headings and fill in whatever you can in ten minutes.

  1. Who depends on me. Children, a spouse, a parent whose bills you pay, the brother who calls you before he calls anyone else, the dog. Anyone whose week would fall apart if yours did.
  2. What I think I own. A rough guess, from memory. The house, the car, the checking account, the 401(k) from the job before last. Don’t look anything up yet. Chapter 2 will show you how close the guess was.
  3. Who I’d call if I couldn’t speak. Not who you’d call to say you’re sick. Who you’d want answering for you, about money and about your body, if you were in a hospital bed and couldn’t. Write a name. If no name comes, write that down too. It’s the most useful blank on the page.

That sheet is the start of your plan. It goes in the front pocket, and everything else gets added behind it.

Get a folder that closes.

Chapter 1: What an Estate Plan Is, and What Happens Without One

Marlene came across the road on the second Saturday in December with a sour cream coffee cake in a foil pan and her reading glasses pushed up into her hair. She set the pan on my counter, right next to the green accordion file, which was open, with the 1996 will poking out of the first pocket and two yellow legal pads beside it.

“What’s all this?”

I told her. Bev, the envelope from the probate court, Jess at the table with her coat on.

Marlene cut herself a piece of her own coffee cake, which she always does, and said, “Well. Estate plans are for people with estates.”

She meant it kindly. She meant that she and I are not the Rockefellers. She has a paid-off house, a checking account, a Malibu with 140,000 miles on it and two grown children who call on Sundays. Nobody needs a lawyer for that. That’s what she meant.

I’ve heard some version of her sentence from at least a dozen people since. It’s wrong, and it’s wrong in a way that costs families months.

Here’s what I told her. Everybody has an estate plan. Every person in this country who owns a toothbrush has one. The only question is whether you wrote yours or your state wrote it for you.

Your state’s version already exists. It’s sitting in the statute books: who gets your house if you die without a will, who a judge appoints to manage your money if a stroke takes your speech, who the doctors turn to when you can’t answer them. Legislators wrote those rules for a family they’d never met. Sometimes the default fits you. More often it fits the way a borrowed coat fits.

Marlene chewed on that, and on the coffee cake. “So who’d get my house?”

“I don’t know,” I said. “Neither do you. That’s the whole problem.”

I meant it. I’ve been through three estates at our county courthouse and I couldn’t have recited the rule for a widow with two children and no will. It depends on the state, and the honest answer was that she’d have to look it up. What I could tell her was that she could find out, and that once she knew, she could change it.

Two jobs, not one

Most people hear “estate plan” and picture a will being read aloud in a room with wood paneling. That’s half of it. In my experience it’s the less urgent half.

A plan does two jobs. It says what happens to your things, and to your children, when you die. And it says who acts for you if you’re alive but can’t act for yourself: after a stroke, a car wreck, a fall on the basement stairs, or during a long illness that takes your judgment before it takes anything else.

People plan for the first job and skip the second. I understand why. A death is one event, and you can picture it. Incapacity is murky, it arrives without a date, and nobody wants to imagine being the one in the bed. But it’s the job that tends to come due first. My mother needed someone who could legally sign for her two years before she needed anyone to read her will.

The American Bar Association’s page on powers of attorney puts the risk plainly. Without one, a court may need to appoint a guardian or conservator to manage your affairs, and you may not get to choose who it is. Think about that for a minute. A court case, so somebody can pay your electric bill. A judge deciding which of your children is the responsible one.

Write both halves.

The five pieces

There’s no official list, and every lawyer arranges it a little differently. But in the three estates I’ve handled and the one plan Dale and I finally made, the core came down to the same five pieces of paper. I’ll name each one here and leave the details to the chapters that own them.

A will. It names the person who will settle your estate, says who gets what passes under it, and lets you nominate a guardian for children who are still minors. It controls less than most people think, and Chapter 4 is about exactly how much less.

A durable financial power of attorney. This names someone, called your agent, who can handle money for you while you’re alive: pay the mortgage, talk to the bank, deal with the tax return. “Durable” means it keeps working after you lose the ability to manage things yourself, which is the whole point of having one. The choices inside it are in Chapter 7.

A health care power of attorney and a living will. Two documents, sometimes on one form. The first names the person who makes medical decisions when you can’t. The second writes down what you’d want them to decide. The National Institute on Aging calls these the two most common kinds of advance directive. Chapter 8 covers them.

Your beneficiary forms and account titles. You don’t sign these in a lawyer’s office. They’re the pages on file at your bank, your 401(k) plan, your life insurance company, and the exact wording on your deed. They often move more money than the will does, and they don’t care what the will says. Chapters 2 and 3 are about them. I count them as part of the plan, not as bank paperwork, and by Chapter 3 you will too.

A letter of instruction and an inventory. Neither is a legal document. The inventory is the list of what you own and where it lives. The letter is plain English to the people you leave in charge: who to call first, where the spare key is, who takes the dog. Chapter 2 builds the inventory, and Chapter 12 puts the letter together.

You’ll notice a living trust isn’t on that list. That’s on purpose. Some people need one, and plenty of people are sold one who don’t. Chapter 6 helps you tell which you are.

When I read the five to Dale that night, he counted them off on his fingers.

“Five pieces of paper,” he said. “I’ve done harder furnace installs.”

He wasn’t wrong. None of the five is hard to understand. The hard part is deciding, and then actually signing, and most people stall at the deciding.

What your state does if you don’t

Here is the default plan, the one you already have. It comes in three pieces, and each is a different kind of trouble.

If you’re alive but can’t act

Say you have a stroke next March. You’ll live, but for some months you can’t read a bank statement or sign your name.

Your checking account doesn’t know that. The mortgage still comes due, the property tax bill still arrives, and the bank will not let your husband or your daughter move money out of an account in your name alone because they love you and they’re standing right there. Without a financial power of attorney, the path the ABA describes is a court: a guardianship or conservatorship, with a judge picking the person and, depending on your state, ongoing reports to the court about how your money is spent. You might like the person the judge picks. You don’t get to be asked.

Medical decisions work a little differently, and the default here can be gentler. According to the National Institute on Aging, if you don’t have an advance directive, your state’s law decides who speaks for you, and that’s typically a spouse, parents or adult children. If you’re married and your spouse knows your wishes, the default may roughly match what you’d choose.

But look at who isn’t on that list. The NIA specifically warns that an unmarried partner who isn’t named could be left out. I know a couple of people in their sixties who have been together twenty years and never married, for perfectly good reasons. Under that default, a sister in another state may have more say in a hospital hallway than the person who’s been sleeping in the chair next to the bed. The same goes for a stepchild who’s been doing the driving to appointments, or a close friend who knows exactly what you’d want.

The default also says nothing about what happens when three adult children disagree. They get to sort it out among themselves. In a hospital hallway. At two in the morning.

If you die

Without a will, you die “intestate,” which is the word I heard over supper as a girl. It means your state’s law of descent and distribution writes the will for you. The ABA’s introduction to wills and Cornell Law School’s Legal Information Institute both describe the same basic pattern: property typically goes to a spouse and children first, then to parents, siblings and more distant relatives, in an order your state sets. The shares and the order vary from state to state, sometimes a lot. That’s why I couldn’t answer Marlene.

Notice that the list is made of relatives. The ABA lists stepchildren, friends and charities among the people a will can provide for when intestacy wouldn’t. If the person you’d want to have the house is the stepson you raised from age six, or the niece who checked on you every Tuesday, the state’s will usually doesn’t know they exist.

Also notice what a missing will doesn’t do. You haven’t named anyone to settle the estate, so somebody still does the job; you just didn’t pick them. And whatever you own by beneficiary form or joint title doesn’t follow the will at all, will or no will, which is what Chapters 2 and 3 untangle. How an estate actually moves through probate court is a different book, The Executor’s Step-by-Step Guide.

Marlene’s other worry, the one she said with her fork in the air, was that “the state takes the house.” It can happen, but it’s narrower than she feared. Cornell’s Legal Information Institute notes that if no relatives can be found, the property can pass to the state. For a woman with two children who call on Sundays, that wasn’t her real risk. If what she actually meant was paying for a nursing home someday, that’s Medicaid planning, a separate subject with its own rules, and the right person to ask is an elder law attorney, not me and not this book.

If both parents die and the children are young

This is the column I’d fill in first if I were you and had kids at home.

Your will is where you nominate a guardian for minor children, if you’re the surviving parent; the ABA lists that among the things a will can do. A nomination isn’t automatic. California’s court self-help site, which I’ll use as the worked example because it explains this so clearly, says a court decides who becomes a child’s guardian even when a parent has nominated someone, after an investigator’s report and a hearing. But the nomination is the strongest word you get. Without one, the judge starts with no word from you at all, and listens to whoever shows up.

Dale and I had a nomination. That was the embarrassing part. Our 1996 will named my parents as Jess’s guardians, and both of them were dead. If Jess had been eight that December instead of thirty-one, our will would have handed our child to two people in the cemetery on Route 50. A judge would have been choosing anyway.

Who to name, how to ask them, and how to keep the money you leave a child from needing its own court case are in Chapter 5.

The tax question, in proportion

When people finally sit down to do this, they usually come in worried about the wrong thing. Marlene was worried about two: the state taking the house, and taxes. Most of the people reading this can set the federal estate tax down right now.

According to the IRS page “What’s New — Estate and Gift Tax,” the basic exclusion amount for people who die in 2026 is $15,000,000. That figure was set by Public Law 119-21, signed July 4, 2025. For 2025 it was $13,990,000. Roughly put, an estate has to be worth more than that before federal estate tax comes into it at all. The figure is per person, it has changed several times in my adult life, and it can change again. When you read this, check the IRS page for the current year.

State taxes are a separate question, and this is where people get caught. Some states charge their own estate tax or inheritance tax, with rules that have nothing to do with the federal number. Pennsylvania is a clear example. According to the Pennsylvania Department of Revenue, as I checked it in 2026, its inheritance tax rate is 0 percent on what passes to a spouse, 4.5 percent to children and other direct descendants, 12 percent to brothers and sisters, and 15 percent to most other heirs. A Pennsylvania family that would never come near a federal return can still owe the state.

So do two things. Search your own state’s department of revenue website for “estate tax” and “inheritance tax,” and write down what you find, with the date. And if your estate is anywhere close to the federal figure, or you live or own property in a state that taxes estates or inheritances and the amounts look real, that’s a conversation for an estate lawyer and a CPA together. This is exactly the kind of question where they earn their fee, and where a book can’t do the math for you.

For everyone else, here’s my opinion. Taxes get the headlines because they make people nervous enough to buy something. In the three estates I’ve handled, not one owed a federal estate tax. What cost us was time: months of waiting, Saturdays of paperwork, letters that each needed a document we didn’t have. The plan is mostly a defense against that.

Tell them before you sign

I promised myself I’d say this once in this book, so here it is.

Most family fights over estates start with silence, not greed.

I’ve sat through a lot of hard conversations across three estates. Exactly one of them was about money. Every other one started some version of the same way: “Why didn’t anybody tell me?” Why is my brother the executor? Why does she get the house? Why did Mom sign that without asking us? People can live with a decision they don’t like. What they can’t stand is meeting it for the first time in a lawyer’s office, after the person who made it is gone and can’t explain.

So apply that to your own plan, while you’re making it. Before you sign, tell the people you’re naming what you’ve chosen and why. Tell the daughter you’ve named as your health care agent, and ask her if she can do it. Tell the son who isn’t executor why his sister is, so he hears your reason in your voice and not in a letter. If you’re leaving one child less because you already helped her buy a house, say so out loud, now, to both of them.

You don’t have to read anyone your account balances. How much of the numbers to share is its own decision, and Chapter 12 gets into it. I’m talking about the choices. The names. The reasons.

Dale and I told Jess what we’d decided at Sunday supper, before we signed anything. She asked two questions. Then she asked for the gravy.

That’s how it should go.

The “If I do nothing” sheet

This is the tool for this chapter, and it’s how you find out what your state’s plan is for you. Take one sheet of paper and make three headings across the top or down the page, whichever you like. Leave room under each.

  1. If I’m alive but can’t act. Who handles my money? Who makes my medical decisions?
  2. If I die. Who gets what I own, in what shares? Who settles my estate?
  3. If I die and my children are minors (or if both parents die). Who raises them? Who manages what they inherit?

Under each heading, write three short lines:

  • What my state does by default. Use the answers from this chapter, then check your own state. Your state court system’s self-help website and your state bar’s consumer pages are good places to start. Searching “[your state] intestate succession” and “[your state] advance directive” will usually get you there.
  • Do I like it? Yes, no, or I don’t know.
  • Which of the five pieces changes it. Will, financial power of attorney, health care documents, beneficiary forms and titles, or the letter and inventory.

That’s it. It shouldn’t take more than twenty minutes, and you don’t need any account numbers yet.

Dale and I filled ours in that night after Marlene went home. Under “can’t act,” both of us wrote “a court” and “no.” Under “if I die,” we wrote “1996 will, out of date.” Under the children column we wrote “Jess is grown” and moved on. If your kids are under eighteen, that column is the one to finish before you go to bed.

Every “no” on your sheet is a reason to keep going. Every “I don’t know” is a question for Chapter 2, or for a lawyer when you get to Chapter 11. Put the sheet in the folder, right behind the one you made before this chapter.

No loose pages.

Marlene took a blank copy home, folded in quarters in her coat pocket. She left the rest of the coffee cake.

Chapter 2: Make the List Before You Make the Plan

The second Tuesday in January, Dale came in from a service call at six-forty with ice in the treads of his boots. He ate a plate of chicken and noodles. Then he sat down across from me at the kitchen table, because I’d told him that morning we were doing it that night.

I had a yellow legal pad and two pens. He had the look of a man who’d rather be changing a blower motor.

“This’ll be quick,” he said. “We don’t own much.”

Two hours and ten minutes later we had twenty-three lines.

Not twenty-three million dollars. Twenty-three things: accounts, policies, titles, the work truck still titled to Dale alone, a savings bond Dale’s grandmother bought him as a boy that nobody had ever cashed. Some of the lines were worth four figures. One was worth about two hundred dollars and took the longest to pin down.

Dale went to bed annoyed. Not at me. At the list.

The guess and the list

Before Chapter 1 I asked you to write down what you think you own, from memory, on one sheet of paper. Go get that sheet.

Now put it next to a fresh one. The second sheet is the real one, and the gap between them is the reason this chapter comes before everything else in the book.

Here’s the order of operations, and I’ll defend it against anybody: you cannot decide who gets what until you know what you have and how each piece already moves. Most people start at the will. They sit down to write who gets the house and the savings, and they never find out that the house and the savings were never going to follow the will in the first place.

That isn’t a trick or a loophole. It’s just how American property works, and almost nobody explains it before they sell you a form.

The only question that matters, asked twenty-three times

For every line on your list, ask one thing:

If I died tonight, what moves this to somebody — my will, the way it’s titled, a beneficiary form, or a trust?

Four possible answers. I started calling it the “road,” because every item you own is already on a road to somebody, whether you’ve looked at the map or not.

The American Bar Association’s introduction to wills says it in flatter language. Property held jointly with right of survivorship, or payable on death, or covered by a life insurance policy or a retirement plan passes by title or by beneficiary designation. It does that regardless of what the will says, unless it’s made payable to your estate.

Read that last clause twice. Regardless of what the will says.

Your will governs the probate road, and the probate road is narrower than people think. It carries property in your sole name with nobody effectively named to receive it, your own share of anything you own as tenants in common, and anything a form sends to your estate on purpose or by accident. For a lot of households that comes to the car, the furniture, the checking account they never put a beneficiary on, and not much else.

Two notes before you panic.

First, none of this is about taxes. Which road an item travels decides who gets it and how fast, not what’s owed on it. Those are separate questions with separate rules, and we put the federal tax question in proportion back in Chapter 1.

Second, this chapter is about your own things, while you’re alive and can still change every answer. Sorting out which road a dead person’s assets already took, and what an executor must then do, belongs to The Executor’s Step-by-Step Guide.

You’re on the easy side of this. You can still edit the map.

The four roads, in plain English

Here’s each one, with the kind of thing that travels on it.

Sole name, nobody named

A checking account with only your name on it. A car titled to you. The coin collection. A savings bond in your name with no co-owner. A house deeded to you alone.

This is probate property. It goes where your will sends it. If you have no will, your state’s rules send it, which is where Chapter 1 came in.

Joint ownership

Two people on the same thing. This is where the exact words matter, and where I see the most confusion.

Joint tenants with right of survivorship means that when one owner dies, the other owner owns the whole thing, automatically, by operation of the title itself. The will does not get a vote. Dale and I own our house this way, and our main checking account.

Tenants in common means each owner has a share, and when one dies that share goes into their estate, to be handled by their will. Same two names on the paper. Completely different outcome.

The deed or the account card says which one you have, and it does not always say it the way you’d expect. Don’t guess. Go read it.

There’s one more joint arrangement to flag tonight and not solve tonight: an adult child added to your account so they can help with the bills. If there’s one in your house, write ASK beside that line and keep going. Chapter 3 is where I explain what it actually does and what to use instead.

Community property

If you live in a community property state, the rules about what belongs to whom during a marriage are different from what most people assume, and that feeds into what you can leave.

According to IRS Publication 555, revised December 2024, the community property states are Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. Alaska, Tennessee and South Dakota have an opt-in election. That’s twelve places where this matters, and if you’re in one of them, write that at the top of your list.

Ohio isn’t one, so Dale and I set it aside. If you’re in Texas or California, don’t. Ask about it specifically when you get to a lawyer, and say the words “community property” so they know you know.

A beneficiary form

A retirement account. A life insurance policy. An annuity. A bank account marked POD, payable on death. A brokerage account marked TOD, transfer on death. In many states, even a deed can be set up to transfer on death — the rules vary a lot, so check your own state before you count on it.

All of these move by a form on file at the institution. Not by your will. Not by fairness. By the form.

Those forms, and the mistakes buried in them, are Chapter 3, which is the chapter I’d read twice if I only had time for two.

A trust

If you have a living trust, it controls exactly what’s been retitled into it, and nothing else. A trust with your name on the cover and an empty inside does nothing at all. Whether you need one, and how funding works, is Chapter 6.

Most readers can write “no trust” on every line and move on. Write it anyway. The blank is the thing that nags at you later.

Where to find the truth

Here is the part people skip. You do not fill in the “how is it titled” column from memory. Not yours, not your spouse’s, and not from a lawyer’s file drawer from 1996.

The house and any other real estate. The deed. Your county recorder’s or auditor’s office holds it, and a lot of counties let you search by name online for free. You want the vesting line — the sentence naming the owners — copied onto your list word for word. If it says “husband and wife,” or “joint tenants with right of survivorship,” or just two names with “and” between them, those can mean different things. Copy it exactly and let the lawyer tell you what it means.

Bank accounts. Call or go in and ask for two things: the exact title on the account, and the name of any payable-on-death beneficiary on file. Ask for it in writing. “In writing” means an email, a printed screen, or a signed form — something you can put in the folder. The teller’s memory and yours are both worthless in nine months.

Retirement accounts. The beneficiary page lives with the plan administrator or the custodian, not with your employer’s HR department and not in your filing cabinet. Most 401(k) and IRA providers will show it to you online in about four clicks. Old plans from old jobs are the problem, and we’ll get to ours in a minute.

Life insurance. The policy itself, plus a confirmation from the insurer of who’s currently named. Group coverage through work counts, and so does the small policy your parents took out on you when you were nine, if it’s still in force.

Vehicles, boats, trailers. The title. Your state’s motor vehicle agency can tell you what’s on it and whether your state allows a beneficiary to be added.

Everything else. Savings bonds, the HSA, the brokerage account you opened during the pandemic, the certificate of deposit at the credit union, the mineral rights your grandfather left, the timeshare, the business, the storage unit.

Ask for it in writing.

What isn’t yours

Two items came off our list that night, and I want you watching for the same thing on yours.

The first was Aunt Bev’s storage unit, which I was unwinding as her executor. The second was a savings bond my mother bought Jess in 1994. That bond had been Jess’s since the day it was issued. Both had been filed in my head under “things I have to deal with,” and that is not the same category as “things we own.”

So I started a second sheet and gave it a heading I’d recommend to anybody: not ours. Property you happen to be handling for somebody else is a job, not an asset, and a job belongs on a different piece of paper. Mixing the two is how people end up leaving things in a will that were never theirs to leave.

Keep the sheets apart.

The one we almost missed

We were at line eighteen when Dale said, “What about the supply house?”

Before he started his own business, Dale worked eleven years at a heating-and-cooling supply house in Columbus. When he left, somebody rolled his retirement money into an IRA at a brokerage firm. That was 2003. Neither of us had thought about it since, except as a statement that came in the mail once a year and went straight into a drawer with the car insurance.

It took us forty minutes to find the account number, and we found it on an old tax document, not a statement.

It became line nineteen. And the question of whose name was on the beneficiary page of a form Dale signed in 2003, back when his mother was alive and Jess was in grade school, is exactly the kind of question Chapter 3 is about. I’ll only say that we didn’t like the answer, and that fixing it took one phone call and eleven minutes.

Twenty-one years of not looking. Eleven minutes to fix.

If you take nothing else from this chapter: the account you haven’t thought about is the account with the problem.

Debts go on the list too

An inventory of only the good things is half an inventory, and it’s the half that makes life harder for whoever comes after you.

Write down what you owe and to whom: the mortgage, the home equity line, the car loan, the credit cards, the medical bills on a payment plan, student loans — including any you took out for a child. Note which ones are in your name alone and which are joint with your spouse, because that distinction will matter to someone someday.

Then add a short section at the bottom that isn’t about money at all. Call it “who to call.” The insurance agent. The accountant who does your return. The guy at the credit union who knows you. The number for Dale’s business bookkeeping software, which I promise you nobody else in this family could find.

That part took me nine minutes and it may be the most useful nine minutes in this book.

Nobody can do this for you

I want to be straight about something, because the rest of this book sends you toward professionals and I don’t want you waiting on one.

A good lawyer will draft documents you couldn’t write yourself. A financial advisor can tell you things about your accounts that I can’t. Neither of them can make this list. They don’t know about the credit union CD. They don’t know your father-in-law co-signed the truck. They can only work from what you hand them, and if what you hand them is incomplete, you will get a careful, well-drafted plan with a hole in it.

This is the one piece of the work that is entirely yours. It’s also the piece that makes everything after it faster and cheaper, because a lawyer billing you by the six-minute increment should be spending those increments on decisions, not on asking you where you bank.

Make the list first.

The asset map

Here’s the tool. One line per item, five things across the page. Use a legal pad, a spreadsheet, whatever you’ll actually keep up. We used the legal pad, then I typed it, then I printed it, because paper is what gets found.

  1. What it is. “Checking account,” “the house,” “Dale’s rollover IRA,” “term life through the union.”
  2. Where it is. Institution and the last four digits of the account, or the county and parcel number for land. Never write full account numbers on a sheet that lives in a kitchen drawer.
  3. How it’s titled. The exact words, copied from the deed, the title or the account record. If you don’t know yet, write “ASK” and the date you plan to ask.
  4. Who gets it if I died tonight. A name, not a wish. “Don’t know” is a legitimate entry and a loud one.
  5. The road. Will, title, beneficiary form, or trust. One word.

Then three lines at the bottom of the page: today’s date, who helped you make it, and where the backup copy lives.

Here’s what to expect, because it happened to us and it’ll happen to you. Your first pass will have “ASK” in column three on about a third of the lines, and “don’t know” in column four on more than you’re comfortable with. That’s not failure. That’s the list doing its job. Ours took three sittings across two weeks to finish, and one of the lines wasn’t settled until April.

Update it once a year. Where it lives and how to keep it current is Chapter 12, and the short version is that it goes in the green file with everything else.

One more thing, and then go get the legal pad.

Dale was annoyed that night, and he was right to be. Twenty-three lines is more than “we don’t own much,” and a fair number of them were pointed at the wrong person or at nobody. We’d been married thirty-six years at that point and we’d never once laid it all out on one page.

Three weeks later he took the list to the garage, where he keeps his good light, and read it again by himself. When he came back in he said, “We should’ve done this at forty.”

Start yours with the line you’re least sure about.

Chapter 3: The Forms That Beat Your Will

The woman at Bev’s bank turned her monitor so I could see it.

It was Wednesday, December 6, 2023, fifteen days after we buried my aunt. I was there on estate business, and the executor’s side of that visit is covered in The Executor’s Step-by-Step Guide. What belongs here is one line on that screen. Bev’s savings account, the one she’d kept at the bank downtown since before I could drive, had a payable-on-death beneficiary on file.

Uncle Roy.

Roy died in 2011.

That account went into probate. With nobody alive on the form, there was no one for the bank to pay, so the money dropped into Bev’s estate alongside everything else she owned in her own name. The estate took fourteen months to close. That savings account waited the whole time, in line with the furniture.

It wasn’t a fortune. It was most of the cash Bev had. And if she had gone back to that bank any afternoon in the twelve years after Roy’s funeral and written one living name on one card, the money would have gone straight to that person, outside the court, the way the form is built to work.

Bev was not careless. She paid her bills the day they came. She just never thought of that card again, and nobody asked her to.

It’s maddening, and I can’t fix hers. You can fix yours.

The form wins

In Chapter 2 you sorted every line on your list by road. This chapter is about the road that carries the most money in most households I know, and the one people check the least.

Here’s what travels by beneficiary form: life insurance, including the group policy through work. A 401(k) or 403(b). An IRA, traditional or Roth. Annuities. A bank account marked payable on death. A brokerage account marked transfer on death.

The ABA’s wills primer puts the rule plainly. These assets pass to whoever is named on the designation, and the will has no say, unless the designation sends them to your estate. I’ll come back to that exception, because people trip on it.

What this means in a kitchen is blunt. Say your will leaves everything to your three children in equal shares. Say your 401(k) still names only your oldest, because she was the only one born when you started that job. If that designation is valid under the plan — which for a married participant usually means a signed spousal consent is on file, and I’ll come back to that — your oldest gets the 401(k). All of it. The will can’t reach over and even things out, and your other two children can’t make her share. She might choose to. That’s a different thing.

A will is a set of instructions for a court. A beneficiary form is an instruction the institution has already agreed to follow, and it follows it without asking anyone what you meant.

When Dale and I counted, nine of our twenty-three lines traveled by form. Apart from the house, those nine lines held most of what we had. I’d always assumed the will was the main event.

It wasn’t even close.

First in line, and the backup

Most forms ask for two kinds of people.

The primary beneficiary gets the money when you die. The contingent beneficiary gets it only if every primary beneficiary has died before you. Bev’s form had a primary and nothing underneath. One name, and when that name was gone, the form had nothing left to say.

Name a backup.

If you split among several people, write percentages, and make them add to 100. I’ve seen a form with three names at 33 percent each, and I’ve seen one with two names and no numbers at all. Both will get sorted out eventually. Neither should have to be.

Then there’s a box a lot of forms offer and a lot of people skip: per stirpes. Cornell Law School’s Legal Information Institute defines it as “by branch.” If a beneficiary dies before you, that person’s share goes down their branch of the family to their heirs, instead of being split among the other people on the form.

Here’s the picture. You name your three children equally, per stirpes. Your son dies before you do. His third goes to his children. Without that box, depending on how the institution’s form works, his third may be divided between his two sisters, and his kids get nothing from that account.

Neither answer is wrong. They’re just different families. Decide which one you want, and then find out what your institution does if you leave the box empty.

Ask for its answer in writing.

One caution before you check the box everywhere: if those grandchildren are small, per stirpes can hand money to a toddler. That runs straight into the first trap below.

Four ways good intentions go wrong

None of these come from greed or carelessness. Every one comes from somebody trying to be kind or trying to keep it easy.

Naming a child under eighteen

A minor can be named and can inherit. What a minor usually can’t do is manage the money alone. The ABA’s introduction to wills, in its section on life insurance, says a policy paid directly to a minor child generally needs a court-appointed guardian or conservator to handle it. That means a court, a process, and somebody reporting to a judge about your grandson’s college money.

The usual fix is to name a trust for the child, or a custodian under your state’s transfers-to-minors law, instead of the child directly. Which one fits your family, and how parents set it up, is Chapter 5. For now, if you find a child’s name in the primary or contingent line of any form, write “ASK” beside it on your audit sheet.

Naming “my estate”

This is the exception I promised. When a form names your estate as beneficiary, the money stops traveling by form. It goes into the probate estate and follows your will — or your state’s intestacy law, if you don’t leave a valid will — and it goes through the court with everything else, which is where Bev’s savings ended up by accident.

Some people do it on purpose because it feels tidy: one document, the will, controls everything. I understand the instinct. But you’ve just taken an asset that could have skipped the court and sent it through the court. Unless a lawyer has given you a specific reason for your situation, name people.

You’ll see in a minute that we had one of these and didn’t know it.

Naming one child to “share with the others”

I’ve heard this one at more kitchen tables than any other. “I put Karen on it. She’ll split it with her brothers. She’s the responsible one.”

She may well be. But once the money is in Karen’s name, it is legally Karen’s. Nothing makes her share it. And even if she wants to, her own life gets a vote: her debts, her marriage, a bad year. There’s also paperwork. The IRS puts the annual gift exclusion for 2026 at $19,000 per recipient. If Karen hands one brother more than that in a year, she’s generally into gift tax return territory, Form 709, and a conversation with a tax preparer. Tax actually owed is unlikely for most families, but she’d be doing federal paperwork for the favor you asked of her.

If you want three children to get equal shares, put three names on the form.

Adding a child to the account “for convenience”

Chapter 2 flagged this one. Here’s the full warning.

When you add your daughter to your checking account as a joint owner with right of survivorship, you haven’t filled out a beneficiary form. You’ve changed the title. And titles beat wills the same way forms do. When you die, the account is hers. The ABA’s introduction to wills notes that these convenience accounts often lead to family disputes and can defeat the plan in the will.

Most people who do this want two separate things and use one tool for both. They want someone to help pay the bills while they’re alive, and they want the account to pass without fuss when they die.

Split the jobs. For bill-paying, a durable financial power of attorney gives your helper access without making the money hers; that’s Chapter 7. For passing the account, a payable-on-death designation naming every child you mean to include does what the joint title was supposed to do, and does it evenly.

If you already have a convenience account, don’t rip it apart tonight. Write it on your list with the exact title words, and bring it to the lawyer.

If you’re married

Two wrinkles, both important, neither one you can fix with a pen at the kitchen table.

First, some workplace retirement plans don’t let you name whoever you like. The ABA notes that for certain retirement plans and spousal annuities, the law requires the surviving spouse to be the beneficiary, and that right can be waived only with the spouse’s properly signed consent. The IRS says the same thing from the plan’s side, on its page about the qualified joint and survivor annuity. A married participant in a qualified plan gets that form of benefit unless the participant and the spouse consent in writing to something else. And the plan has to have a plan representative or a notary witness the spouse’s signature.

A signature at your kitchen table, by itself, may not be worth anything. If you’ve named anyone other than your spouse on a 401(k) or a pension, call the plan administrator and ask three questions: does this plan require spousal consent, is a signed consent on file, and was it witnessed the way the plan requires? Get all three answers in writing.

Note which account you’re asking about. The IRS page is about qualified workplace plans, and an IRA is not one of those, so don’t assume the same protection rides along when money gets rolled out of a 401(k) into an IRA. If that’s your situation and you’re naming someone other than your spouse, ask a lawyer in your state.

Second, if you live in one of the twelve community property places listed in Chapter 2, your spouse may already own part of an account that’s in your name alone, and a form naming someone else can run into that. This is a question for a lawyer licensed in your state.

And if you’ve been divorced: some states automatically cut an ex-spouse out of a will after a divorce. Do not count on that happening on a beneficiary form. The money side of divorce is its own book, Gray Divorce After 50, and I’ll leave it there.

A word about the bank’s insurance limit

This won’t apply to most readers, but it’s worth one paragraph because the rule changed recently and the old version still floats around.

According to the FDIC’s “Your Insured Deposits” brochure, since April 1, 2024 trust accounts at an insured bank, including payable-on-death accounts, are covered at $250,000 per owner for each eligible, distinct beneficiary. The ceiling is $1,250,000 per owner at that bank, for all trust accounts combined.

Those two words are doing real work. Eligible, in the FDIC’s brochure, means a living person, a charity or a non-profit organization. Distinct means each person counts once per owner, no matter how many of that owner’s accounts at that bank name them. So one owner with a savings account naming three children could be covered up to $750,000 at that bank. Name the same three children again on a second account at the same bank and you’ve added nothing. Name a sixth person and you’ve added nothing past the $1,250,000 cap. The account itself also has to meet the FDIC’s requirements. For an informal payable-on-death account, that means the beneficiaries are named in the bank’s own deposit account records.

One more line from that brochure, because it surprised me. If a beneficiary of a payable-on-death account dies, there’s no grace period; coverage usually drops right away.

If your balances are anywhere near those numbers, read the FDIC brochure yourself and talk to your bank. If they aren’t, set it aside.

When to stop and call a lawyer

Most beneficiary forms are a phone call or a login. A few are not, and I’d rather you pay for an hour than guess.

Get a lawyer before you sign the form in four situations. You want to leave a retirement account to a trust. A beneficiary has a disability and may rely on government benefits. You’re in a second marriage with children on either side. Or you’re in a community property state and want to name someone other than your spouse. In each of those, the box you check has legal and tax effects that the form will never explain to you, and the institution’s phone representative usually won’t.

Write those down for Chapter 11.

What Dale’s form said

Back to line nineteen.

The last Thursday in January 2024, Dale and I sat at the kitchen table with the brokerage’s customer service number and his old rollover IRA statement. The representative read us the beneficiary page from 2003.

Primary: me. Fine.

Contingent: Dale’s mother.

She died in 2015. If I had died before Dale, and then Dale had died, that IRA would have had a form with nobody alive on it — exactly Bev’s situation, and the brokerage’s fine print deciding what happened next. I did not want Jess reading fine print in a lawyer’s waiting room.

“Mom’s been gone since 2015,” Dale said. That was the whole of his comment, and it covered it.

The representative walked Dale through the change on the brokerage’s website while we stayed on the line. Me as primary, 100 percent. Jess as contingent, 100 percent. Eleven minutes, start to finish, including the hold music. We printed the confirmation screen before we hung up, and a confirmation letter came in the mail eight days later. Both went in the green file.

That was one of nine. Seven more were fine once we saw them in writing.

The ninth was Dale’s term life policy, bought from an agent in 1998. Primary: me. Contingent: “estate of the insured.” Neither of us remembered choosing that. My guess is the agent filled it in to get the form finished. The insurer wanted a paper change form, signed and mailed. Dale signed it at the kitchen table on a Saturday morning, and the confirmation came the first week of February.

Two wrong out of nine. Both written by younger versions of us, in good faith, about a family that had changed since.

The beneficiary audit

Here’s the tool. It turns the “beneficiary form” lines on your asset map into a short project you can finish in a couple of weeks of evenings.

  1. Pull every form-road line from your asset map. Life insurance, retirement accounts, annuities, POD and TOD accounts.
  2. Ask each institution for the current designation, in writing. A printed screen or a letter. Not your memory, and not the summary page that shows only “beneficiary on file.”
  3. Read it slowly. Check the spelling of every name, that the percentages add to 100, that a contingent is named, and whether per stirpes is checked.
  4. Change it the institution’s way. Online, by phone or on their paper form. A note in your will doesn’t change it. A letter to your lawyer doesn’t change it.
  5. Keep the confirmation. File it in the green folder, right behind the asset map.

Then keep one sheet, one line per form, with these headings:

  • Account (institution and last four digits)
  • Primary beneficiary and share
  • Contingent beneficiary and share
  • Per stirpes: yes, no, or ASK
  • Date of the last change
  • Confirmation filed (date and where)

The “date of the last change” column is the one that tells you the most. Ours had 2003 and 1998 in it. If yours has a year that starts with 19, start there.

When to look again

A form is only as current as the last time you touched it. Pull the audit sheet out whenever one of these happens:

  • Anyone named on a form dies
  • You marry, or a beneficiary does
  • A divorce, yours or a beneficiary’s
  • A birth or adoption in the family
  • A beneficiary runs into money trouble or a serious illness
  • You open a new account or change jobs
  • You move to another state

Chapter 12 puts this sheet on the yearly March list too, so it gets looked at even in a year when nothing happens.

Bev’s card outlived Roy by twelve years. Somewhere in your files there’s a form with a name on it you haven’t thought about since the year you signed it.

Find the oldest one. Call that one first.

Chapter 4: Your Will: What It Does and What It Can’t

My father’s will was three typed pages in a blue paper cover, stapled once in the top left corner. I read it at my mother’s kitchen table on a weekday afternoon in 2016, with Helen across from me not reading it, and Kevin on a plane from Tucson.

Page two, about a third of the way down, there was a line I still think about.

“I give my Buick to my son, Kevin.”

Dad sold that Buick in 2009. He sold it to a man who went to the same church, for less than he should have, and he was pleased with himself about it for a week.

The will was signed in 1994. He died twenty-two years later. In between, he sold the car.

So the line did nothing. There was no Buick. The sentence sat there on page two, legally harmless, and it wasn’t harmless at all, because Kevin got off that plane and read it and decided something. He decided that a car had gone missing, or that Dad had changed his mind about him, or that somebody should have told him. I’m not sure which, and I’m not sure he was either. He asked me twice that week whose name the Buick had been in.

Twenty-two years is a long time for a piece of paper to sit in a drawer while the world rearranges itself around it.

What your will actually reaches

You already know the shape of this from Chapter 2. The road a will controls is a narrow one, narrower than most people assume.

The ABA’s wills primer puts the boundary in one sentence: your probate estate consists only of the assets subject to your will, or to your state’s intestacy laws if you don’t have one. The accounts and policies that travel by form, which were Chapter 3, are somewhere else entirely. So is anything held jointly with a right of survivorship.

This is why I put the will fourth in this book instead of first.

A will is still worth doing. It does several things that no form, no title and no trust will do for you. But if you came here expecting the will to be the document that settles everything, lower that expectation now, tonight, while you can still act on it.

What only a will can do

Here is the honest list, drawn from that same ABA page.

It names your executor. Somebody has to be in charge. If you don’t name a person, a court picks from whoever steps forward. The ABA also notes that in your will you can relieve your executor of the bond requirement, and that in some states naming an independent executor, or waiving certain state statutes, cuts down how much the court supervises the settlement of your estate. That’s a real saving of time and friction, bought with one sentence drafted by a lawyer who knows your state.

It nominates a guardian for children still at home, where you are the parent who outlived the other one. The nomination is not the same as the appointment, and the whole subject — who to pick, how to ask them, how to keep a child’s money from the court — is Chapter 5. Don’t try to solve it from this chapter.

It gives things to people the state would skip. Intestacy rules follow bloodlines and marriage. They don’t know about your stepson who’s been yours since he was four, your godchild, your neighbor who drove you to every appointment for two years, or the animal shelter on the county road. The ABA names stepchildren, godchildren, friends and charities specifically. If any of those are in your plan, they’re in your plan because you wrote them into a will.

It says who gets the rest. The residue is the part people forget and the part that matters most. More on that in a minute.

It can create a trust at your death, which is how parents keep a child’s inheritance out of a teenager’s checking account. That’s Chapter 6.

It can name a successor custodian for a child’s or grandchild’s transfers-to-minors account, so a court doesn’t have to appoint one.

Five of those six are invisible. They don’t feel like they’re worth the trouble, right up until the day somebody needs them.

Write gifts that survive twelve years of your life

Dad’s Buick line is the most common mistake in homemade wills, and I’ve seen versions of it in lawyer-drafted ones too. You name a thing. Then your life goes on and the thing doesn’t.

Four rules I’d give anybody.

  1. Give percentages and shares, not objects, for anything that matters financially. “Forty percent of the residue to my daughter” works whether the money is in a credit union, a brokerage account or a coffee can in 2041. “My Buick to Kevin” works for exactly as long as you own a Buick.
  2. Define the residue and then look at it hard. The residue is everything left after the specific gifts, the debts and the expenses. For most households it’s the great majority of the probate estate. If your will spends two pages on the silverware and one line on the residue, you’ve written the wrong will.
  3. Name a backup taker for every gift. What happens if the person you named dies before you do? A well-drafted will answers that for each gift and for the residue. If yours doesn’t, state law answers it, and state law has never met your family.
  4. If you do name an object, say what happens when it’s gone. A lawyer can draft the gift so that it quietly disappears, or converts to a dollar amount, or passes to the next person in line, if you no longer own the item at your death. Say what you want out loud at the meeting and let the drafting handle it.

For the furniture and the jewelry and the tools, the ABA says that in some states a will may refer to a separate memorandum covering tangible personal property, which you can change without re-signing the whole will. It also says to proceed with caution, because a memorandum that contradicts the will, or gets written sloppily, creates the exact confusion it was meant to prevent. Ask whether your state allows one. Then ask your lawyer whether, for your family, it’s a good idea.

Those are different questions. People who ask only the first one end up with an unsigned list in a drawer and two siblings who both remember being promised the dining table.

Choosing your executor

The job, in one sentence: gather what’s in the estate, pay what’s owed, file what the court and the tax people require, hand out what’s left, and report on all of it. For the full picture of what you’re asking of somebody, I wrote a separate book about that side of it, The Executor’s Step-by-Step Guide.

What you need from this chapter is how to pick.

Organized beats smart. Available beats far away. Willing beats obligated. The best executor I’ve watched work was a retired school secretary who had never owned a stock in her life and who kept a spiral notebook with the date and outcome of every phone call she made. The worst was a genuinely brilliant man who could not make himself open the mail.

Two more things.

Don’t default to the oldest child because they’re the oldest child. Birth order is not a qualification, and picking that way sets up the one sibling who was never asked to resent the one who was never given a choice.

And ask the person. Out loud, in a conversation, before you sign. I’ve never heard of anybody being offended by the question. I’ve heard plenty of stories about people finding out at the funeral home that they were in charge.

Then name a backup, because people get sick, move, and die in the wrong order.

Leaving your spouse out may not do what you think

This one surprises people, so here it is flat.

In many states, leaving a spouse out of your will does not necessarily disinherit them. State law may let the surviving spouse claim a statutory share, so take this plan to a lawyer licensed in your state. The ABA puts it this way: your right to dispose of property as you choose may be subject to forced heirship laws of most states that prevent you from disinheriting a spouse and, in some cases, children. Many states do it through what’s called a spousal right of election, which lets the surviving spouse claim a certain interest in your estate regardless of what your will provides.

Cornell Law School’s Legal Information Institute, in its July 2024 entry on the elective share, says these statutes exist to prevent the disinheritance of a spouse and give the survivor a fixed fraction, typically out of the deceased spouse’s probate estate. It adds that the traditional fraction is one-third regardless of the length of the marriage, and that elective share statutes are enacted in separate property states. Your state’s fraction may be different, and what it is measured against may be different too.

If you live in one of the community property states or opt-in states listed back in Chapter 2, the analysis starts somewhere else again, because part of the property may already be your spouse’s during the marriage.

Here’s what I want you to do with that. If your plan involves leaving a spouse less than everything — which is normal and often sensible in a second marriage — that is a lawyer conversation, not a form conversation. Same if you intend to leave an adult child out. Leaving someone out without discussing the reason with your lawyer can invite questions or a challenge. Tell the lawyer who you’re leaving out and why, in plain words, at the first meeting, and let them tell you what your state allows and what the drafting should say.

Second marriages and stepchildren have their own chapter, Chapter 10, because the whole picture there is different.

Signing it is not a formality

This is the part that makes a will a will, and the part people rush.

Wills must be signed in the presence of witnesses, with the formalities followed, or the ABA says the will may be invalid. Not “may be questioned.” Invalid. And it adds something worth sitting with: even when a badly executed will is eventually held up, fighting that challenge can be costly and difficult. The cheap fix is to sign it correctly the first time.

The number of witnesses and who may serve varies by state. Look yours up, or have the lawyer’s office run the signing, which is what they do all day.

In many states, the ABA says, a will executed in front of witnesses with all the signatures notarized is “self-proving,” meaning it can go to probate without hunting down a witness years later to testify. If your state offers that, take it. The witnesses to my parents’ 1994 will were a neighbor and a woman from Dad’s shop, and by 2016 one had died and the other had moved to Florida.

Changing a will later: a codicil is an amendment, and it has to be signed with the same formalities as the will itself. The ABA warns that a codicil creating ambiguity with the will it amends causes problems. My opinion, and I’ll own it: for most people, most of the time, a new will is cleaner than a patched old one, because there’s one document instead of a document plus a sheet of paper that has to be found with it. Ask the lawyer to quote both options before you decide.

About handwritten wills, because somebody always asks. Cornell’s Legal Information Institute explains that a holographic will is written and signed in the testator’s own handwriting and, by definition, doesn’t need witnesses. It also says some states don’t recognize them at all, and that the requirements vary a great deal where they do. Their own examples make the point. Texas requires the will to be written wholly in the testator’s handwriting. Utah accepts one if the signature and the material portions are handwritten. New York recognizes it only from armed forces members in actual service during a conflict, people serving alongside them, or a mariner at sea.

Read that spread again. Three states, three different answers.

So don’t rely on a handwritten will. Some states reject it outright, and the states that accept it impose different requirements, which means the page you write at the kitchen table on a bad night may turn out to be no will at all. Follow your state’s signing rules, or have a lawyer in your state run the signing.

Whether you need a lawyer at all for the will itself, and how to keep that bill down, is Chapter 11. One line here: this is the document where I’d spend the money.

The will decision sheet

Here’s the tool. It’s one page, and it exists so that your first meeting is about judgment instead of data entry. Write it in pencil. Argue about it with your spouse at the kitchen table, not in front of a lawyer at six-minute increments.

  1. Executor, and backup. Full name, relationship, city, phone. Note whether you’ve asked them yet, and the date you did.
  2. The residue, in percentages. Who gets the rest, and how much each. The numbers must total 100.
  3. Backup takers. For each person above: if they die before me, their share goes to ___. Their children? The other people on the list? Say it.
  4. Specific gifts. Keep this list short and keep it off the money. For each one: the item, the person, and what happens if I no longer own it.
  5. People intestacy would skip. Stepchildren, a partner you’re not married to, friends, charities. Names and what you want them to have.
  6. Anyone you mean to leave out, and one sentence on why. This sheet goes to the lawyer. It does not go in the will unless the lawyer says it should.
  7. Guardian nomination, if you have minor children. Leave it blank for now and come back after Chapter 5.

Then the three lines that go at the bottom of every sheet in this book: today’s date, who you worked on it with, and where the copy lives.

Dale and I did ours on the first Sunday in February 2024, after the beneficiary forms were sorted and before the rest of it. Forty-five minutes, and forty of them were spent on item three, because we had never once said out loud what should happen to Jess’s share if Jess died before us. It turns out we agreed. We just hadn’t known that.

Put the sheet in the folder behind the beneficiary audit.

* * *

I never did answer Kevin’s question about the Buick properly. I told him Dad sold it in 2009 and showed him the line in the checkbook register, and he nodded, and that was the end of the words about it.

A few months later he said something on the phone that I’ve kept. He said the car wasn’t the point. The point was that a sentence written when he was twenty-six had been sitting in a drawer telling him something that stopped being true when he was forty-one, and nobody, including Dad, had thought to go back and look.

Go look at yours.

And if you don’t have one to look at, start the decision sheet with item one: write down who’s going to be in charge, and who’s second.

Chapter 5: If You Have Children: Guardians and Money for Minors

Owen went down at seven in the porta-crib in the back bedroom, the one that used to be Jess’s, and came awake twice before nine. It was a Saturday in February 2024. Marcus had made two trips to the car for the diaper bag and the sound machine and the particular blanket.

We were at the kitchen table with the last of the pot roast pushed to one side when Jess said they’d finally done their wills. A lawyer in Dublin, a Tuesday evening appointment, both of them in work clothes.

I said good. I meant it.

Then she said, “We named Tanya.”

Tanya is Marcus’s sister. She lives in Hilliard, eleven minutes from their house. She has two kids, eight and five, in the same school district Owen would start in.

I want to be straight with you about the next four seconds, because this chapter is not useful if I pretend. I felt it in my chest. Not anger. Something smaller and worse than anger, the thing you feel when you find out you weren’t the obvious answer to a question you didn’t know had been asked.

Dale, drying his hands on the dish towel, said, “She’s closer to the school.”

And he was right, and I knew he was right before he finished saying it. I was fifty-nine that February. Owen was two. If something took both Jess and Marcus the following year, I’d have been sixty at the start of it and seventy-five on the day he finished high school, and Dale would still have been crawling under furnaces to pay for whatever came after. Tanya was thirty-four. Tanya’s kids would walk Owen to the bus stop.

I told Jess she’d picked right. It took me about a day and a half to stop feeling the other thing, and I’m not sure I’d have managed it at all if she hadn’t thought to ask me to be the backup.

Ruth and Dale’s own will decision sheet from the week before had item seven left blank, because our child is a grown woman who teaches seventh-grade science. So this chapter isn’t our story. It’s the one I’d have wanted at thirty-two, and the one Jess read a draft of.

Two jobs, and nobody says they’re the same person

The word “guardian” is doing two different jobs, and families lose whole arguments to that confusion.

The California Courts self-help guide lays out both plainly, and I’m using California as a worked example all the way through this chapter because its courts publish the process in public and in English. Your state will differ. Go find your own state court’s self-help pages before you sign anything.

A guardianship of the person means an adult who isn’t the child’s parent has the legal right to make decisions about that child’s life and the responsibility for their care: medical decisions, what school they go to, housing, food, clothes, safety. That’s the person who raises your child.

A guardianship of the estate means someone is appointed to manage the child’s money. California’s guide says this one is needed when a child has a lot of money, income or property — for example, money inherited from a parent who died. It also says guardianships of the estate have very strict rules about how the money is handled, what lawyers call fiduciary duties, and that it’s usually best to have a lawyer’s help with one.

Read those two paragraphs again and notice they describe different skills.

The sister who will get up at two in the morning with a feverish eight-year-old is not automatically the person you want filing an annual accounting with a probate judge. Sometimes she is. Often she isn’t, and that’s not an insult to her. You can name different people for the two jobs. Most families don’t realize they’re allowed to.

You nominate, and then a judge appoints

Your will nominates. That’s the actual verb, and the gap inside it matters.

The ABA’s introduction to wills says you may designate a guardian for your minor children if you are the surviving parent, and that doing so minimizes court involvement in the care of your child. Minimizes. Not eliminates.

Here’s what the court side looks like, again using California’s published process. Someone files a petition and pays a filing fee. California’s detailed filing instructions listed $225 for a person-only petition and $435 for an estate-only or combined petition when I checked them in October 2026, and said a few counties charge $35 to $50 more. Confirm the exact amount with your court before you go. The child’s parents and other relatives have to be served with the papers and the hearing date. Even relatives who consent can change their minds and show up to object. Before the judge decides, the court appoints someone to investigate whether the guardianship is necessary and write a report. Then there’s a hearing where the parents and other family members get to speak. Then the judge decides.

And if the guardianship is granted, it doesn’t end there. California requires the guardian to send the court an update every year on the child’s health, education and where the child is living.

Your nomination records your choice, but the judge applies state law and decides whom to appoint. It is not an order. Which means two practical things.

First, the nomination has to be in a will that was signed correctly, or it may never be read at all. Everything in Chapter 4 about witnesses and formalities applies to this sentence more than any other sentence you’ll write.

Second, both parents should nominate the same people. Two wills naming two different aunts is a gift to a judge who has never met either of them. If you and the other parent genuinely disagree, have that fight at your own table, in February, with coffee. Do not outsource it.

Name a backup, too. Your first choice could be sick, overseas, or gone. Jess and Marcus named Tanya, and then me and Dale behind her, and that second line cost them one extra sentence of drafting.

Choosing, with the sentiment taken out

Here’s my opinion, and it’s the one that makes people at church look at me sideways.

Grandparents are the sentimental choice and frequently the wrong one.

I say that as the grandmother who got passed over and then agreed with the decision. Do the arithmetic before you do the feelings. Take your child’s age today, subtract it from eighteen, and add that many years to the person you’re considering. If the answer is a seventy-three-year-old driving a sixteen-year-old to swim practice at five in the morning, think harder. There are plenty of exceptions — grandparents of forty-eight who are already raising kids are a different proposition entirely — but run the number instead of assuming.

The rest of what I’d weigh, in rough order of how much it ends up mattering:

Who already knows your child’s actual life. The teacher’s name, the allergy, the way he gets about thunderstorms. Transition is the thing that hurts a grieving child, and the person who needs the least briefing causes the least of it.

Where they live. School district, the friends your kid already has, how far from the other side of the family. Moving a child two states away from everyone who knew their parents is a second loss stacked on the first one.

The weather inside their own household. Their marriage, their money, their health, how many children they already have and how old. This is uncomfortable to assess about people you love. Assess it anyway.

Whether they’ll say yes and mean it. Some people cannot say no to a dying friend’s request and then cannot carry it. You want the one who’ll ask you three hard questions before agreeing.

One more thing that lawyers see and ordinary people don’t. If you’re naming a married couple, say what you mean. Is your choice Tanya, or is it Tanya-and-her-husband as a unit? What do you want if they divorce, or if one of them dies first? Tell your lawyer which, and let the will say it. A will that names “my sister and her husband” and then goes quiet is a will that leaves a judge guessing in the worst year of your child’s life.

You can also write down what you care about — faith, schooling, keeping the kids together, contact with the other side of the family. Say it, and understand that a judge isn’t bound by it. Write it anyway. It tells the court and the guardian who you were.

The conversation you have to have out loud

This is the first half of the tool, and it isn’t a form. It’s a conversation, and it has an agenda.

Ask it in person, not by text, and not at a holiday table with eleven people in the room. Jess and Marcus asked Tanya on her back patio in October 2023, before they’d seen the lawyer, which is the right order.

What to ask them:

  1. Would you do this, knowing it probably never happens?
  2. Does your spouse or partner agree? I’d like to hear them say it.
  3. Where would the kids live — your house, or would you come to ours?
  4. Is there anything about your own situation in the next five years that I should know about? A move, a health thing, a job that travels.
  5. If it ever stopped being workable for you, would you tell me?

What to tell them, in the same sitting:

  1. There will be money, and here’s roughly how it’s set up, so you aren’t raising my child out of your own pocket. (You don’t have to say the balance. You have to say that it exists and who controls it.)
  2. Who I’ve named as backup, and why.
  3. Where the papers are, and who to call first.
  4. That I’ll check in on this every year and they can change their answer.

Then write the date of that conversation on your will decision sheet, next to the name. A nomination nobody has agreed to is a guess.

Ask them in person.

The money is the other half, and it’s the half people skip

Chapter 3 said it in one line and I’m picking it up here. A minor can inherit. A minor usually cannot manage what they inherit. The ABA’s wills primer says insurance proceeds payable directly to a minor child generally make a court appointment of a guardian or conservator necessary. That’s the second kind of guardianship from the top of this chapter, with the annual filings and the strict rules.

Then there’s the part that makes parents sit up. Without a trust or another arrangement, court or custodial control may end when the governing state law says the child can take control. In California, the court’s self-help guide says a guardianship ends automatically when the child turns 18. That controlling age can differ from your state’s general age of majority, and it can differ by account type. Ask your lawyer what it is for each account your child could inherit.

Legal adulthood doesn’t mean a young beneficiary is ready to manage a large payout. Picture your own eighteenth birthday with a life insurance check in your hand, and be honest about what you’d have bought.
