The ABA addresses this directly, and it’s the most useful paragraph on that page for young parents. Trusts aren’t only for the wealthy. Many young parents with limited assets create trusts, during life or in their wills, so their children’s money is held until an age the parents consider mature enough, often older than the age of majority. The ABA also describes something most people have never heard of. The money can be held as a single undivided fund, used for the support and education of the children according to what each of them needs. It gets divided among them only when the youngest reaches a specified age.

Think about what that does. Three kids, aged fourteen, ten and four. A rigid equal split on the day you die gives the fourteen-year-old four years of support and the four-year-old fourteen years of it, out of the same-sized pile. The undivided fund treats them the way you would have: whoever needs braces gets braces.

So the choices in front of you, in plain terms, are three. A trust created inside your will. A living trust you set up now. Or a custodial account under the transfers-to-minors law your state has adopted. How trusts actually work, what they cost you in bother, and whether you need the living kind at all is Chapter 6, and I’m not going to pre-empt it here. What belongs in this chapter is the sequence.

Set up the arrangement first. Then point the beneficiary forms at it.

That order is where families go wrong. Somebody meets with a lawyer, agrees to a trust for the children, signs everything, and leaves the two-year-old’s name sitting in the beneficiary box of the life insurance policy from work, where it has been since open enrollment. The form still wins. It always wins. Pull your audit sheet from Chapter 3 and check the line for every policy and account that would pay out if you died tonight.

One more small thing from Chapter 4’s list, if you’re already holding money for a child or grandchild in a custodial account of that kind. Your will can name your successor custodian, which saves a court appointment. Ask for it by name at the meeting. It’s one line of drafting and most people never think to request it.

Two situations where you stop and call a lawyer first

A child or adult heir with a disability who receives, or may someday receive, needs-based government benefits. Money landing in their name can cost them the benefit you were trying to supplement. A direct inheritance can disrupt needs-based benefits. Get advice from a lawyer who handles benefits planning before naming this beneficiary anywhere: a will, a trust or a beneficiary form.

A stepchild. Intestacy laws follow bloodline and marriage, so a stepchild you’ve raised since he was four is generally not an heir unless you name him. Chapter 4 made that point about wills. It cuts harder on the guardian question, because in a blended household there may be another living parent whose rights outrank your nomination entirely. Chapter 10 takes the whole picture apart.

The guardian letter

The will handles the legal part in a sentence. This handles the Tuesday.

It isn’t a legal document, nobody files it anywhere, and it’s the thing a guardian would actually read at eleven at night in the first week. One page per child, handwritten is fine, kept with your plan and a copy with the person you named.

  • Medical. Pediatrician and dentist, with phone numbers. Allergies. Prescriptions and the pharmacy. The insurance card’s location. Any specialist, and what the last appointment was about.
  • School. District, school, grade, teacher, bus number. The IEP or 504 plan if there is one, and where the paperwork lives.
  • The day. Bedtime, the routine around it, the food they’ll actually eat, what they’re afraid of, what calms them down.
  • People. Best friends and their parents’ phone numbers. The coach. The other side of the family and how much contact you want. Anyone you’d rather they not be left alone with, and no, you don’t have to explain it on paper.
  • Money. Who controls the children’s money and how the guardian reaches them. Not account numbers.
  • What I’d want. A short paragraph in your own words about faith, schooling, keeping siblings together, and anything else you’d say if you had five minutes. Written to the guardian, not to the court.

Put the date at the bottom and both parents’ initials beside it, and note on your will decision sheet where the copy sits. Then redo it when it stops being true, which for a small child is about once a year.

* * *

I wrote mine anyway.

Not as the guardian. As the backup behind Tanya, which is a job that mostly consists of being reachable. One page, in the green file, about a two-year-old who hates the sound of the vacuum and will eat anything if it has cheese on it. Most of it will be wrong by the time he’s five, and I’ll write it again.

Jess asked me once whether it bothered me, being second. I told her the truth, which is that it did for a day and then it stopped, because the only question that mattered was who gets Owen to school on Monday.

If you have a child under eighteen and no name written down anywhere, that’s tonight’s work. One name, one backup, and a phone call to ask.

Chapter 6: Living Trusts: Who Needs One and Who Doesn’t

The flyer came to Marlene’s house, not ours, which tells you something about the mailing list.

Cream card stock. A photograph of a gray-haired couple on a porch swing that nobody’s grandchildren have ever sat on. Across the top, in a font pretending to be handwriting: Protect Your Home. Protect Your Legacy. Lunch Is On Us. The steakhouse out on Bridge Street, a Thursday at noon, the last week of February 2024.

She walked it across the road and put it on the counter next to the salt shaker and said she wasn’t going alone.

So we went.

They had set out forty chairs in the back room and nineteen of them filled, counting us. I was the youngest person there by a decade, which at fifty-nine was a new experience. Chicken or sirloin. The iced tea came in those amber plastic tumblers. A pleasant man in a good jacket stood at the front with a remote in his hand and talked for fifty-one minutes.

I counted the word “probate” nineteen times. I counted the questions he asked us about what we actually owned.

Zero.

That is the whole problem in one number. The slides were written before any of us walked in. So the answer at the end of them came out the same for the retired schoolteacher with a paid-off house, the farmer with two hundred acres and a son in Indiana, and Marlene, who has a checking account and a Malibu. Nineteen people, nineteen different sets of facts, one recommendation. A plan shaped before anybody asks what you own isn’t a plan. It’s a product.

There was a sign-up sheet by the door and a man with a tablet taking appointments for the following week. He quoted a price at our table, and I’m not going to print it, because one man’s number in one steakhouse in one Ohio county in February 2024 tells you nothing whatsoever about what a lawyer in your town would charge you. If a number ever shows up in this book, you’ll get the year and the source along with it. That one has neither.

We left without signing. In the parking lot, with her coat buttoned wrong, Marlene asked me the question you’re holding this chapter to ask.

“So do I need one of those or not?”

I told her I didn’t know yet. Then I told her the more useful thing, which is that neither did he.

What the thing actually is

Strip the porch swing off it and a revocable living trust is a legal arrangement you set up while you’re alive. The American Bar Association’s page on revocable trusts puts it plainly: the trust is legally in existence during your lifetime, it has a trustee serving right now, and it owns property that you have transferred into it. You are usually that trustee yourself, sometimes alongside a co-trustee. You manage your own property, for your own benefit, exactly as you did before, and most of these trusts are written so you can amend or revoke them whenever you want.

Then two things can happen.

If you become unable to handle your own affairs, the trustee named to step in is authorized to manage the property and spend it on you and your family. If you die, that successor trustee either hands the property to the people you named or keeps holding and managing it for them, according to the instructions you wrote.

There’s a second animal with a similar name. An irrevocable trust can’t be revoked or changed, and the ABA says it’s done almost exclusively to produce particular tax or asset-protection results. That one is lawyer territory from the first sentence, and if anyone at a lunch seminar suggests it, stand up. I’m talking only about the revocable kind in this chapter.

Notice what the definition does not contain. No porch. No protection from anything. It’s a box with a name on it, a person responsible for the contents, and instructions.

Everything useful about it depends on what’s in the box.

What it is genuinely good at

I want to give the trust its due before I take the air out of the sales pitch, because the ABA is more enthusiastic about living trusts than the seminar was, just for different reasons.

Somebody can manage your money if you can’t, without a judge choosing them. This is the one the flyer didn’t mention once. A will does nothing while you’re alive. A funded trust gives your successor trustee authority over the property in it the day you can’t exercise it yourself, which avoids having a guardian appointed for that purpose. The ABA’s probate page goes further than I expected. It says a properly prepared and administered living trust is a very effective tool for managing assets through illness, disability or the effects of aging. It then adds that, with an aging population, using trusts to reduce the risk of elder financial abuse deserves to be an important consideration in a plan. The strongest official endorsement I found for living trusts is about being alive, not about dying.

Property in a second state. If you own real estate somewhere other than where you live, pay attention to this one. Cornell’s Legal Information Institute, in its entry on ancillary administration last reviewed in June 2021, explains that estate assets located in a state other than where the person lived need a proceeding in that state too, because each state has its own property laws. Two states, two court processes, two sets of fees, two lawyers who’ve never met. A cabin in Michigan or forty acres in Kentucky titled into a trust travels differently.

Holding money for an heir who shouldn’t get it all at once. If money needs to be held for a child or an adult beneficiary, reread Chapter 5. Here, the question is whether a living trust is the right vehicle; take that question to a lawyer.

Delay. California’s court self-help site says the fastest probate can happen in California is typically nine months. That’s the fast version, in one state, according to that state’s own courts. If your state’s process runs like that and your family would be waiting on the house, the trust is buying something real.

What it does not do

Now the other column, and this is where the lunch was being paid for.

It does not save estate tax. Not a dollar. The ABA says so in a single sentence: revocable trusts don’t help you avoid estate tax, because your power to revoke or amend the trust keeps the property includable in your estate. If anyone tells you a revocable living trust reduces your taxes, you have learned something valuable about that person and nothing about trusts. Chapter 1 covered what the federal figure is and where to check it, and most readers of this book are nowhere near it anyway.

It does not control anything you didn’t put in it. I’ll come back to this because it’s the failure I’d bet on.

It does not finish the job by itself. The ABA states that a living trust can almost never totally avoid probate, and that a simple will is still needed to “pour over” into the trust any property you didn’t transfer during your lifetime. So the trust doesn’t replace your will. It adds a document and keeps a shorter one. Anybody selling you a trust as the thing that lets you skip a will is selling you the wrong thing.

It does not delete the work. One line from the ABA’s probate page deserves to be read out at every free lunch in America. The basic job of administering and accounting for assets has to be done either way: by an executor in probate, or by a trustee because everything sat in a living trust. Somebody still inventories, still pays, still files. And much of the delay people blame on probate comes from tax laws and tax filing requirements, which a trust does not eliminate.

It is not free, before or after. Property passing through a trust has to be moved in, administered by a trustee who may or may not charge fees, then moved back out to the beneficiaries. The ABA notes there can be other costs along the way too, such as real estate transfer taxes or fees, depending on where you are.

Privacy is a maybe, and it’s state-specific. You’ll hear that a will becomes a public record and a trust doesn’t. Whether that matters in your state, and how much of a probate file the public can actually see, is a question for a lawyer licensed where you live. Ask it as a question. Don’t buy it as a fact.

Funding is the whole job

If you take one thing from this chapter, take this.

A trust controls what has been retitled into it. Nothing else.

That means the deed to the house has to be re-recorded in the trust’s name, at the county, with whatever your state requires. The brokerage account has to be reopened or re-registered in the trust’s name. The bank has to change the title on the account. Every piece has its own paperwork, its own clerk and its own waiting period, and the retirement accounts need their own careful handling, because naming a trust as the beneficiary of an IRA or a 401(k) has tax consequences that are genuinely complicated. Don’t do that part off a template. Ask the lawyer, in the meeting, what should happen to each account by name.

Here’s how it goes wrong, and I’ve watched it twice.

Somebody pays for a trust. They get a handsome binder with a blue cover and gold lettering, and in the back there’s a list of transfers to complete. The binder goes on a shelf. Six years later the deed is still in their own name, the accounts are still in their own name, and the trust owns one dollar that somebody put in to open it.

An unfunded trust is the most expensive empty folder a family can buy.

So when you ask a lawyer about a trust, the real question isn’t what the document costs. It’s this: who does the funding, is it included, and will I get a written list of what still needs to move, with a date on it? Get the answer before you decide, not after. And before any retitling, ask the institution and your lawyer whether the change affects that account’s beneficiary designation, and request the answer in writing. Then walk every line of the audit sheet from Chapter 3 again.

Ask who does the funding.

Probate in proportion

The seminar’s entire engine was fear of probate, so let’s look at what the lawyers’ own association says about it.

The ABA’s probate page says most probate proceedings are neither expensive nor prolonged, and then says out loud what I’d been thinking in the back room of that steakhouse: that this is contrary to the claims of many vendors selling living trust products. It adds that many states have simplified or streamlined their probate processes, and that in those states there’s less reason to use probate-avoidance techniques unless you have other valid reasons.

It also makes the point that reframed this for me. In planning your estate, more important than minimizing probate is minimizing the things that make probate difficult in the first place, like lawsuits among the heirs.

Probate laws differ in every state. In some states court and attorney fees are set by statute; in others they’re minimal. A well-drafted will can cut out some of the steps in many states. A comparison between the cost of probate and the cost of a trust has to be made case by case, which is a sentence that will never fit on a flyer.

So “does a trust avoid probate” is the wrong question. The question is what probate costs and how long it takes where you live, and whether that’s worth what the trust costs you in money and bother. In California, by that state’s own account, nine months is the fast lane. In a state with a streamlined small-estate process and a house that passes to a surviving spouse by the title, you may be paying to avoid three months and a filing fee.

Find out which state you’re in. Literally.

Does a trust earn its keep

Here’s the decision rule Dale and I used, and the one I gave Marlene on a sheet of notebook paper. It doesn’t give you an answer. It tells you whether you have a real question to take to a lawyer or a sales pitch to walk away from.

Count how many of these are true for you.

  1. I own real estate in more than one state.
  2. Someone has to be able to manage my property for me if I can’t, and I’d rather that person be named by me and ready to act than appointed by a court.
  3. Money needs to be held for somebody rather than handed to them: a child, a young adult, an heir who can’t manage money, or an heir on needs-based benefits.
  4. A local lawyer has told me that probate in my county is slow or costly for an estate like mine.
  5. I expect a fight. Ask a lawyer licensed in my state what parts of probate are public and whether a trust would change that for my property.
  6. A good part of what I own has no beneficiary form available and no joint owner, and the only road it can travel is through the will.

None true, or one? You probably don’t need one, and you certainly don’t need one this Thursday from a man with a tablet.

Two? Put those two facts on your asset map and ask a local estate lawyer one question: what would a trust solve here that my will and financial POA would not? Do not buy one at a seminar before you get that answer.

Three or more? You have a genuine question. Take this list to an estate lawyer, say which items you checked and why, and ask them to tell you in plain terms what the trust would do for those specific facts. Then ask what it would cost to do nothing. A lawyer who won’t answer the second question isn’t advising you.

And whatever you decide, the arrangement belongs in the asset map from Chapter 2, with a date, because future-you will not remember why.

What we decided, and what would have changed it

We said no.

Our facts: one state, a house we own together with a survivorship title, retirement accounts and insurance that travel by the forms we’d just spent January fixing, one adult daughter who teaches seventh-grade science and is married to a man who alphabetizes his tools. On my six questions, Dale and I checked exactly one, and it was number two, and Chapter 7 is about the cheaper document that handles it.

Sam confirmed it in about four minutes in April and then charged us for four minutes, which is what I wanted. He didn’t talk us out of a trust. He asked what we owned, in what state, titled how, and then said that for us it would be paperwork we’d have to maintain for twenty years to solve a problem we didn’t have.

Here’s what would have flipped us, and I want you to see how small the changes are.

If Dale’s uncle’s cabin in Michigan had ever come down to us, we’d have a trust. One cabin, two states, and I know what two court processes feel like.

If Jess had died before us and Owen had become our direct heir at four years old, we’d have a trust, and Chapter 5 says why.

If either of us had a condition that made a bad year likely rather than possible, we’d have a trust, because the ABA’s best argument for one is about managing property while you’re still here.

That’s the honest shape of this decision. It isn’t about how much you own. It’s about where it sits, who’s going to receive it, and whether you’d be comfortable with a judge picking the person who handles your checkbook.

Marlene checked none of the six.

She called me from her kitchen the next week to say a woman from the seminar had phoned her twice. The second time, Marlene told her she’d decided to spend her money on a will, a power of attorney and a health care form, and asked to be taken off the list.

Then she asked me whether that was all right.

It was more than all right. A seventy-one-year-old widow with a paid-off house and two children who call on Sundays does not need a binder with gold lettering. She needs four signed documents and a drawer her kids know about.

If you’ve been carrying a flyer like Marlene’s around in your coat pocket, go read my six questions and count. Then put the flyer in the recycling or put it in the folder with a note about which numbers you checked.

Either one beats a Thursday at the steakhouse.

Chapter 7: Financial Power of Attorney: The Document You’ll Need While You’re Alive

My mother had the paperwork. That’s the part that still gets me.

Helen spent most of her working life as a paralegal at a law office downtown. She knew the words. She had a financial power of attorney drawn up properly in 2009, signed with witnesses and a notary, three copies, one of them in a fireproof box in her bedroom closet under the winter blankets. When Dad died in 2016 she took that box out, checked that my name was still on the document, and put it back.

In March 2017 she fell in her own kitchen reaching for the coffee filters on the top shelf. Hairline fracture in the left wrist. In the emergency department somebody noticed she couldn’t name the month, and a nurse said the word “infection” in a kind voice, and some of that confusion cleared over the following week and some of it never did.

She came home with a brace, a folder of appointment cards, and no interest whatsoever in her mail.

Three weeks later I found a pink shut-off notice from the electric company in the stack by her toaster, under a church bulletin and two seed catalogs.

So I drove to her bank on a Tuesday morning with her power of attorney in a manila envelope, feeling, I’ll admit, a little smug about being the daughter who had the document.

The teller got the branch manager. The branch manager read it twice, turned to the second page, and put his finger on a paragraph I had never read carefully. Mom’s document was a springing one. It took effect only on the written determination of two licensed physicians that she could no longer manage her own affairs.

He wasn’t being difficult. He was reading the instructions my mother wrote.

Her doctor of nineteen years had retired the year before. The one who inherited the practice would not write a letter about a patient he’d met once, which is defensible, and the first opening he had was eleven days out. The second physician’s letter came from the hospital, by fax, after I called four times. Then the bank’s own people needed to look at both letters.

Twenty-three days from the pink notice to the morning I could pay my mother’s electric bill.

I paid it out of my own checking account that first week, along with her supplemental insurance premium. Two checks, $271.64, and I never asked anybody to pay me back, and that was never the problem. The problem was the twenty-three days.

Here is the part I want you to sit with. Mom chose springing on purpose. She had watched, from a desk at a law office, what a few agents did with immediate authority over somebody else’s money, and she didn’t want a document floating around that let anyone touch her accounts while she was perfectly capable of writing her own checks. Her instinct was sound.

She just never found out what the trade cost.

What this one piece of paper does

A power of attorney lets you name someone to act for you in money matters while you are alive. That’s the whole idea. The American Bar Association’s page on the subject says it is accepted in all states, though the rules and requirements differ from one state to the next, and the person you name is called your agent or your attorney-in-fact.

The document can be narrow or wide. The ABA describes a power limited to one particular activity, like closing the sale of your house while you’re out of the country, or general in its application, which is the kind most people mean when they’re planning. It can take effect the moment you sign it, or only when something happens later, usually a determination that you can’t act for yourself. That second kind is the springing one that cost my mother and me three weeks.

Your agent has only the authority the document gives. And in a lot of situations the agent has to physically produce the paper to use it. The ABA’s examples are the ones I’ve lived: the motor vehicles department wants to see it before honoring a signature on a title, a title company wants it for real property, a broker or banker wants it before selling securities or opening and closing accounts. Signing checks for you is usually the exception where nobody asks.

There’s a second document with a similar job in the medical world. It names who speaks for you about your care rather than your money, and it is Chapter 8’s entire subject. Two documents, two different jobs, often signed the same afternoon. Don’t let anyone tell you one covers the other.

The word that does the actual work

Durable.

A durable power of attorney stays good after you become incapacitated. Cornell’s Legal Information Institute, in its durable-power-of-attorney entry last reviewed in January 2022, says the durability has to be explicitly stated, and that a non-durable one, meaning a document without that provision, ends the moment the principal is incapacitated.

Read that sentence backward and you’ll see why it matters. A power of attorney without durability language stops working at exactly the point where you most need somebody to be able to act. It’s a document for conveniences, not for crises.

The ABA says most states today permit a durable power that remains valid once signed until you die or revoke it. Some older state rules required renewal; some people’s documents include a termination date on purpose, which the ABA notes is done to reduce the risk of a former spouse or a former friend still holding authority years after the friendship ended.

When your lawyer hands you a draft, find the sentence that says the document survives your incapacity. Point at it. Ask them to read it out loud.

If it isn’t there, you don’t have what you came for.

Why we picked immediate, and why you might not

Dale and I signed immediate powers for each other. No physician letters, no triggering event, no certification clause. The day we signed, each of us could have walked into the credit union and moved the other’s money.

That sounds reckless written down. Here’s the reasoning.

The man I’d be handing that authority to has slept beside me for thirty-eight years and has never once spent money without telling me, including the time he bought a used sheet metal brake at an auction and confessed before he got it in the truck. If I can’t trust Dale with immediate authority, a springing clause is not going to save me. It’s going to delay him by twenty-three days on the worst month of my life, and the person who takes advantage of an immediate power is rarely stopped by a paragraph requiring letters.

That’s my opinion and it comes with a condition attached: it only holds if your agent is the right person. If you are naming somebody because they’re the oldest, or because they live closest, or because you’d feel awkward not naming them, the springing clause is not your fix either. Pick a different agent.

Some people still choose springing for real reasons. You might be naming an adult child you trust but whose spouse you don’t know well. You might be in a second marriage where the children of the first marriage are going to read everything you sign. You might just hate the idea on principle, the way Mom did.

If you choose it, do this: make the trigger as easy to pull as your lawyer will let you. One physician instead of two. A named doctor rather than “two licensed physicians” in the abstract. A written standard for what the letter has to say. Ask your lawyer what their certification clause actually requires in practice, and ask how long it has taken their other clients to satisfy it.

Then call your doctor’s office and ask whether they write those letters at all, and what they charge, and how long it takes. Do that before you sign, not in the week of the pink notice.

Picking the person

The ABA is blunt about qualifications, and I’d put this on a card: there are no special qualifications to act as an attorney-in-fact, except that the person must not be a minor or otherwise incapacitated. That’s the legal floor. It is a very low floor.

The sentence worth copying out is the next one. “Integrity, not financial acumen, is often the most important trait of a potential agent,” the ABA says on that same page.

I believe that more every year. The bookkeeping can be learned in an afternoon or bought from an accountant. Honesty under pressure, when nobody’s watching and your mother’s savings account is sitting right there, cannot be bought at all.

Two structural points the ABA makes that people skip.

Name successors. Always. Your agent may be unavailable or unable to act when the time comes, and if you named one person and nobody behind them, you’re back to the courthouse. Name a second. Name a third if you have one.

And if you name two people to act at the same time, say in the document what happens when they disagree or when only one is reachable. The ABA points out that co-agents may not all be available and may not agree, and that the designation should indicate whether you want a majority to act. Two adult children named jointly, in a family where they already argue, is not fairness. It’s a stalemate with your checkbook in the middle.

Tell them, out loud, before the signing. Not because the law requires it. Because the first time someone learns they’re your agent should not be at a hospital information desk.

Then hand them something to read. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau publishes free booklets called “Managing Someone Else’s Money.” There’s a separate one for each kind of financial caregiver, and the one you want is the version written for an agent named in a power of attorney. It’s a PDF on consumerfinance.gov, and the page was last modified in June 2026. It costs nothing, it’s written for ordinary people, and it explains fiduciary duty better than I can in a chapter about something else.

Dale printed the agent one and read it at the kitchen table with a pencil. He underlined one line about keeping the money separate and said he was going to need a notebook.

The powers worth arguing about

A general power of attorney covers the daily machinery: deposits, bills, insurance, taxes, the mortgage. The interesting questions are at the edges, and your lawyer will ask about them if they’re any good.

Gifts. Your agent can make gifts for you, subject to the guidelines you write into the document. Some states permit it by statute; others require explicit authorization in the paper itself. If gifting matters in your plan, say so expressly, with limits. One caution: the ABA’s page still illustrates annual exclusion gifts with a figure from 2013. Use the current year’s number from the IRS page Chapter 3 pointed you to, and let your lawyer draft the language, because the ABA warns that a badly drafted gifting power can create estate tax consequences nobody intended.

Changing how things are titled. This one deserves your full attention. The ABA notes that even without touching your will, an agent can affect who ends up with your assets by changing the ownership of them. Remember the four roads from Chapter 2. An agent with title-changing authority can move an asset from one road to another. That can be exactly what you want, or a disaster, depending entirely on who’s holding the pen.

Trusts. Some jurisdictions let an attorney-in-fact create or amend trusts for you during your lifetime, or transfer your assets into a trust you already set up. If you went through Chapter 6 and decided a trust earns its keep, this clause is how the funding keeps happening if you can’t do it yourself. The ABA says it is prudent to state clearly in the document whether you want your agent to have these powers.

What your agent can never do. Revise your will. That’s not on the menu in any state.

Your digital accounts. Whether your agent can get at your email, your photo storage and your online-only bank depends on language in the document and on a body of law I’m giving its own chapter. Ask for it; see Chapter 9 for what to ask for.

Two more things from the ABA that are easy to miss. The law of the state where you live when you sign generally governs what your agent can do. And if you own real estate or valuable property in another state, check with a lawyer that your document reaches it.

Will the bank take it

This is the question nobody asks and everybody later wishes they had.

A perfect document that your bank won’t honor is a stack of paper. Institutions have their own review processes, and some of them want their own form signed alongside yours. The time to find that out is while you’re healthy enough to sign whatever they want.

So call. Ask the branch, and your brokerage, and whoever holds the retirement accounts, what they require to accept a power of attorney, whether they have their own form, and how long their review takes. Write the answers and the date on the asset map from Chapter 2. If an institution says it will want its form, get the form now.

Copies matter too. Your agent needs to be able to put their hands on the document the day it’s needed, which is Chapter 12’s job, but the short version is that a document only you can reach is a document nobody can use.

And know how to undo it. Most states require written notice of revocation to the person you named, according to the ABA, so revoking is not a matter of tearing up your copy and feeling better. If your agent is a spouse and the marriage ends, or a friend and the friendship does, talk to your lawyer the same month.

One more thing, since Chapter 3 already walked you through the trap: adding a child to your checking account is not a substitute for any of this. It’s a title change with permanent consequences. A durable power of attorney is the tool that does the bill-paying job without handing anyone an inheritance by accident.

Seven questions before you write a name

Answer these on paper, in the green file, behind the will decision sheet.

  1. If this person had access to everything I own tomorrow and nobody was checking, would I sleep?
  2. Can they do a boring, repetitive job for possibly years without quitting?
  3. Will they say no to a relative who asks for money, in writing, and take the phone call that follows?
  4. Do they live close enough, or deal well enough with institutions by phone, to spend a morning at a bank branch?
  5. Who is second, and who is third, and have I asked them too?
  6. If I’m naming more than one person, have I said in the document whether a majority can act?
  7. Have I told this person out loud, given them the CFPB guide, and written down the date I asked them?

Three or more uneasy answers and you have the wrong person, not the wrong document. Keep looking. A good agent who isn’t family beats a bad one who is.

The sheet you leave behind

The document gives your agent authority. It doesn’t tell them where anything is. That gap is why competent, willing agents spend their first two weeks on hold.

So write one page, date it, and clip it to the signed document. Not a legal document itself. A map.

  • Which bills pay themselves automatically, from which account, and on what day of the month.
  • Which bills arrive on paper, and where the mail piles up.
  • The institutions by name, with a phone number and the last four digits only, pointing back to the asset map rather than repeating it.
  • Who to call first: the lawyer, the accountant, the insurance agent, and the one neighbor who notices things.
  • Anything that will break if it’s missed for thirty days. The crop insurance. The storage unit. The quarterly estimated tax payment.
  • What I’d want done with the house if this goes on longer than a season.

That last line is the one people leave off, and it’s the one my mother and I never discussed.

The alternative to all of this is a courtroom. The ABA says it plainly. Without a power of attorney, if you become unable to manage your own affairs, a court may have to appoint someone to act for you. Your state calls that person a guardian, a conservator or a committee. And in that proceeding, the ABA notes, you may not have the ability to choose who it is. The same page adds that for some people, extra protection against having a guardianship imposed comes from also having a revocable living trust, which is the question Chapter 6 asked you to answer.

The morning the bank finally said yes, I paid my mother’s electric bill in about four minutes at a desk with a glass partition, and then I sat in the parking lot for a while with my hands on the wheel.

Call your bank this week and ask what it wants to see. Then write down what they tell you, with the date, and put it where your agent will find it.

Chapter 8: Health Care Directives: Who Speaks for You When You Can’t

The resident couldn’t have been thirty. He came around the curtain at two in the morning with a clipboard against his hip and asked the room who could make decisions for Helen.

There were three of us in that ICU bay. Me, a nurse adjusting something on the pole, and my mother, who had been admitted that afternoon in 2018 and had not said a word I could understand since about six o’clock.

I said I could, and then I did the thing I’d been carrying around in my handbag for two years without ever using it. I took out a folded sheaf of paper, four pages, soft at the creases, and handed it over.

He read the first page standing up. Then he said, “Can I copy this?” and walked it down to the station himself.

That’s the whole story. There’s no twist in it. A twenty-minute conversation happened with me instead of around me, and three hours later we made a decision together that I still think was the right one, and my mother never knew any of it took place.

I’ve told the hard version of our family’s paperwork failures twice in this book already. This is the one where the paperwork worked. It worked because Helen was a paralegal who’d signed the thing in 2009 alongside her financial power of attorney, and because I had gotten into the habit, after Dad died, of moving it from one purse to the next.

Four pages. Soft at the creases.

Two documents, two different questions

The National Institute on Aging describes advance directives as legal documents that give instructions for medical care and take effect only if you can’t communicate your own wishes. That last part is the piece people get wrong. Signing one changes nothing about today. Nobody gains any say over your care while you can still speak for yourself.

The NIA names the two most common kinds, and the split between them is the whole architecture.

A living will says what. It tells doctors how you want to be treated if you can’t make your own decisions about emergency treatment, which common treatments you’d want, which you’d avoid, and under what conditions each answer applies. The American Bar Association’s page on health directives is worth reading before you sign one. It points out something most people don’t consider: some commonly used clauses in living wills may forbid assisted breathing, including a device you might already be using for a condition like COPD. Never sign a form handed to you as the standard one until you’ve read it and confirmed it says what you mean.

A health care power of attorney says who. The NIA calls the person your health care proxy, and you’ll also see representative, surrogate and agent. The ABA notes that normally one person is appointed, not several acting at once, though it’s common to name one or more alternates if your first choice can’t be reached.

You can have a proxy without a living will. The NIA says so plainly: a proxy can be chosen in addition to or instead of a living will, and having one helps with the situations nobody can write down in advance, like a stroke or a bad wreck.

My own view, and it’s only mine: if you’re doing one, do both. The living will tells your proxy what you meant. The proxy handles the decisions no form anticipated.

The default, and who it leaves out

Chapter 1 gave you the short version of what happens with no directive. Here’s the rest of it, because the rest is where people get hurt.

The NIA says that without a directive, your state’s laws determine who may make medical decisions for you. Typically that’s your spouse, your parents if they’re available, or your adult children. With no family at all, the NIA says some states allow a close friend who knows your values to help, and otherwise a physician may be assigned to represent your best interests.

Read the gaps in that.

An unmarried partner who hasn’t been named could be excluded from the decision-making, which the NIA says outright. “Some states allow” a close friend means other states don’t. And that last clause about an assigned physician is the one I’d tape to the refrigerator of anyone who tells me they don’t need this. Your best interests, decided by a doctor meeting you for the first time, from your chart.

The NIA’s advice for finding out what your own state does is to contact your state legal aid office or your state bar association. Ask whether they offer free information, or legal help you might qualify for. Do that before you decide this doesn’t apply to you.

Picking the person who’ll be standing there

The qualities are not the same as the ones in Chapter 7. A financial agent needs to be dogged and honest on the phone for months. A health care proxy needs to be able to say one sentence out loud in a corridor at two in the morning while people in scrubs wait for an answer.

Two things to screen for.

Will they do what you asked, even when they’d choose differently? The ABA says to confirm before appointing someone that they will in fact be willing and able to carry out your wishes, and it gives a specific example: if your preferred proxy holds a religious view that prevents them from carrying out your wishes, name someone else. That isn’t a judgment about the person. It’s a kindness to them. Don’t hand a job to someone who’ll have to violate their own conscience to do it.

Second, can they be reached? Name alternates. The ABA treats successors as standard practice, and the hospital will work down your list.

Notice what isn’t on the list. Not the oldest. Not the one who lives closest. Not the nurse in the family, though a nurse in the family is handy for translating afterward. The person who can hold the line is the person you want, and they may be the one who cried least at the last funeral, which tells you nothing about how much they loved anybody.

Ask them out loud. Then ask the alternate.

What the paper can’t make happen

An advance directive is legally recognized but not legally binding. That’s the NIA’s own phrasing, and I’m quoting it because I’ve watched two families discover it the hard way.

What it means in practice: your provider and your proxy will do their best to respect your directive, and there may be circumstances where they can’t follow it exactly. You might be in a complicated medical situation where nobody can tell what you would have wanted. That’s not a failure of your form. No form covers everything.

The NIA also lists three grounds on which a health care provider might refuse to follow your directive: the provider’s conscience, the institution’s policy, or accepted health care standards. If that happens, the NIA says the provider must inform your proxy immediately and consider transferring your care to another provider.

Your proxy should know that sentence exists. It’s the difference between feeling powerless at the desk and knowing what to ask for next.

The orders a doctor writes

A living will is your document. A medical order is the doctor’s.

The NIA treats these as a separate category, and the distinction matters in an emergency. A do not resuscitate order goes into your medical chart and tells staff in a hospital or nursing facility not to attempt CPR or other life-support measures if your heart and breathing stop. The NIA notes that even if your living will says you don’t want CPR, it’s still helpful to have the DNR in your medical file when you go to a hospital. Without the order, staff will attempt every effort to restore your breathing and heart rhythm.

There are relatives of the DNR. A do not intubate order covers the ventilator. A do not hospitalize order tells long-term care staff you’d rather not be sent to a hospital at the end of life. An out-of-hospital DNR alerts emergency medical personnel outside a hospital.

Then there’s the POLST, or MOLST depending on your state, also called a portable medical order. The NIA describes these as forms that give guidance health care professionals can act on immediately in an emergency, as a medical order in addition to your advance directive. They’re typically created when you’re near the end of life or critically ill and you understand the specific decisions likely to come up. Your state department of health can tell you whether these forms exist where you live.

If you’re healthy and doing your planning on a Tuesday night at the kitchen table, you probably don’t need any of these yet. You need to know the words, so that when a doctor says “POLST” to you in four years you don’t nod at something you’ve never heard of.

Getting the forms without paying for anyone’s markup

You can establish your advance directives for little or no cost. That’s the NIA again, and it’s one of the few places in estate planning where free is also correct.

Many states have their own forms. The NIA’s list of places to find them starts with your State Attorney General’s office and your local Area Agency on Aging, which you can reach through the Eldercare Locator at 800-677-1116. The NIA also points to downloads from AARP, the American Bar Association, and the National Hospice and Palliative Care Organization’s CaringInfo. If you’re a veteran, your local VA office has an advance directive written for veterans, VA form 10-0137.

You don’t need a lawyer for this. The NIA says a lawyer can help but isn’t required, and adds that if you have one, give them a copy. There are also outfits that will sell you a form online. Before you pay anybody, remember the list above.

One caution from the NIA that applies to any form you find online: check that it’s legally recognized in your state, and check that the website is secure before you type anything personal into it.

A lawyer can help with your state’s signing rules and with whether a separate HIPAA authorization belongs in your plan. But the NIA is clear that you don’t need one to create the directive.

Signing it so a hospital will take it

Generally these documents require at least two adult witnesses. That’s the ABA, and the rest of its witness guidance is a list of people who usually can’t serve.

Most states restrict who may witness. Generally, witnesses can’t be anyone entitled to an inheritance from you, by will or by state law. Often state law also bars anyone related to you by blood or marriage, or anyone responsible for paying your medical bills. And some hospitals and other medical institutions have a policy against letting their employees witness the signing. Worth knowing before you plan to do this from a hospital bed.

Some lawyers recommend notarizing as well as witnessing. Ask yours.

Two more from the ABA. All states recognize these documents, but the law varies on whether a state will recognize a document prepared in another state. You don’t need extra paperwork for a vacation. But if you spend a considerable part of the year living in more than one state, consider having the documents prepared in each one, and keeping a copy in each place.

Changing your mind takes more care than tearing up paper. The ABA’s page says you can destroy the documents you have and create new ones, but that only handles the copies in your own hands. Your proxy has one. So does your doctor, maybe a hospital, maybe a registry. And states set their own revocation rules. California’s Probate Code, section 4695, is an example: you can revoke most of a directive in any way that shows you mean it, but revoking the person you named as agent takes a signed writing or telling your supervising health care provider in person.

So look up your own state’s rule before you change anything. Then tell your proxy and your doctors, replace any registry copy, and write “revoked” and the date on every old copy you can get back before you hand out the new one.

The privacy law that stops families at the desk

Here’s the paragraph I wish somebody had explained to me in 2018.

Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule, the person with legal authority to make health care decisions for you is your “personal representative.” The Department of Health and Human Services says a covered entity must treat that person as if they were you, both for uses and disclosures of your protected health information and for your rights under the Rule. HHS’s guidance on personal representatives, last reviewed in January 2024, lists a health care power of attorney among the examples for an adult, along with a court-appointed legal guardian and a general or durable power of attorney that includes the power to make health care decisions.

HHS also says the personal representative stands in your shoes and can exercise your rights, including access to your information to the extent it’s relevant to the representation.

Pay attention to that last clause, because it has teeth. HHS gives an example: a person holding a limited health care power of attorney about only one specific treatment, such as the use of artificial life support, is your personal representative only for health information relating to that decision. Narrow document, narrow access.

Many lawyers add a separate HIPAA authorization alongside the directive anyway, naming the people who may receive information even if they aren’t the ones deciding. Whether you need one is a question for a lawyer in your state, not a rule I can give you. Ask yours.

Five questions to answer out loud

The form is half of this. The other half is a conversation most families schedule for never.

The NIA opens its advance care planning page with a finding from one study: people guessed nearly one out of three end-of-life decisions for someone close to them incorrectly. Not because they didn’t care. Because they’d never been told.

So sit down with the person you’re naming, at your own table, with coffee, and answer these five out loud. Write the date on the directive afterward.

  1. What does a good day look like to me now, and what would have to be gone before I’d say it stopped being my life?
  2. If a treatment could extend my life but not get me back to that, do I want it tried, tried for a set period, or not started?
  3. Where do I want to be at the end if there’s a choice: home, hospital, somewhere else?
  4. Who else should be in the room, and who should not be told anything until it’s over?
  5. If you had to go against what my sister wants in order to do what I asked, could you?

Question five is the one that decides whether you’ve picked the right person. Watch the face, not the answer.

Then talk to your doctor. If you have Medicare Part B, Medicare.gov says it covers voluntary advance care planning as part of the “Welcome to Medicare” visit and the yearly “Wellness” visit. You owe nothing there if the provider accepts assignment. Get it during other treatment and the Part B deductible and coinsurance apply. Ask before the visit which one you’re booking. With private insurance, the NIA says to check with your insurer.

Where the copies go

A directive nobody can find is a directive you didn’t sign. Six places, and this list goes in the green file behind the agent sheet from Chapter 7.

  • Your proxy, and each alternate, with the date you gave it to them.
  • Your regular doctor, for your medical records.
  • The hospital, at admission. Take it with you and let them put a copy in your file.
  • Your lawyer, if you have one.
  • Your own file at home, where a responsible adult knows to look.
  • Your state’s registry, if yours has one. The NIA notes some states keep them for quick access by providers and your proxy.

Two habits on top of that. The NIA says to think of these as living documents you review at least once a year and update after a major life event: retirement, a move out of state, a real change in your health. And when you replace a version, the NIA says to file and keep the previous one and note the date it was replaced, and to make sure any registry has the latest. That fits the revocation step above: the old copy stays in your file, marked, so nobody ends up holding two papers with no way to tell which came last.

That goes on the March list in Chapter 12.

Mom’s four pages were in a hanging folder in her closet until 2016. After Dad died, I asked for a copy and put it in my purse, and I moved it from that purse to the next one three times without really thinking about why.

I still don’t know what made me keep doing that. But I know what the resident saw at two in the morning, and I know he stopped looking around the room for somebody else.

Make the copies this week. Hand a paper copy to your proxy in person and ask where they’ll keep it so they can reach it fast. Then do what the NIA suggests and put a card in your own wallet saying you have a directive and where the current copy is kept.

Chapter 9: Passwords, Phones and Photos: Planning for Your Digital Life

In March of 2024 I was clearing out the cabinet above the kitchen phone, the one with the dead batteries and the church directory from two addresses ago, because the drawer with our plan in it had stopped closing properly.

Taped inside the cabinet door was a yellow sticky note. Dale’s handwriting, the squared-off kind he uses on invoices. It said DALE EMAIL and then a word and four numbers.

I know roughly when he wrote it, because he switched to that email address the year the shop got a second truck. Call it 2012.

I stood there with a trash bag in one hand and tried it on my own laptop. It worked.

Dale came in from the garage, looked at the note, looked at me, and said, “Well, there it is.” He was not embarrassed. He was pleased he’d found it.

That is the whole problem with digital accounts, in one square of adhesive paper. The information a family needs is either written somewhere a burglar could find it in ninety seconds, or it is nowhere at all.

Why this part doesn’t work like the rest of your plan

Everything else in this book moves by one of four roads. Your will, the title on the thing, a beneficiary form, or a trust. We spent Chapter 2 sorting your property onto those roads.

Your email does not travel any of them.

Three reasons, and they stack. First, you don’t own most of these accounts the way you own the truck. You agreed to a company’s terms, and those terms say what happens when you die. Second, federal privacy law treats the contents of your messages as something a company may not hand out to whoever shows up with a sad story. Third, and this is the one that surprises people: having the password does not make it legal to use the account. Under the state laws I’m about to describe, a person handling your affairs is specifically not allowed to pretend to be you.

So the sticky note solves nothing, even when it works. A family member who logs in as Dale and starts answering his email is doing something the law in a lot of places does not permit, with a password the company never agreed to let them have.

What you want instead is permission, recorded where the company will honor it.

The law, in plain English, with the caution it needs

A model law called the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act has been enacted in a number of states. I am not going to tell you how many, because I could not verify the count from a source I trust, and I’d rather give you nothing than a number you repeat at a kitchen table.

I can show you what it says where it has been adopted. Washington’s version sits at RCW 11.120. Florida’s is chapter 740 of its statutes. Both are free to read on the state’s own website, and I’m using them as examples of how these rules read, not as the law where you live.

Four pieces matter to you.

The online tool can win. In Washington and Florida, a direction you give through a company’s built-in tool overrides a contrary will, trust or power of attorney, if the tool lets you modify or delete that direction at all times. That condition is in both statutes, and it matters. Where it’s met, a setting you clicked in 2022 can beat a document you signed in front of two witnesses in 2026.

If there’s no online tool, your documents can speak. You can allow or prohibit disclosure in your will, your trust or your financial POA. That’s language your lawyer adds, and it costs you one sentence of conversation to ask for it.

Content is different from the list. The actual text of your emails and messages generally requires your consent, given in one of the ways above, or a court order. A catalogue of electronic communications, meaning who you exchanged messages with and when, is treated as less protected. In these two states the company must disclose the catalogue unless you prohibited it or a court directs otherwise. To receive a catalogue that is available, the personal representative must first send what the statute requires: a written request, a certified death certificate, certified proof of their court appointment, and account details if the company asks.

There are limits and a clock. A fiduciary may not impersonate you. And in Washington and Florida a company has sixty days to comply, counted from when it receives the information the statute requires.

Now the caution. Not every state has these rules, the details differ where they exist, and even in a state that has them, access still depends on the company’s own process, the documents it demands and its terms of service. A statute telling a custodian to comply does not mean the person on the other end of the help form knows that.

To find yours, search your legislature’s website for your state’s name plus “fiduciary access to digital assets.” Or write it on the list for the lawyer in Chapter 11, which is where I put it.

Use the switches the companies already built

Where your state’s law gives a changeable online-tool direction priority, use that tool first, and then make the will and the POA agree with it. Where it doesn’t, the switch still tells the company what you wanted, which is more than silence does. Either way it’s free and it takes minutes, so start there tonight, with the two accounts most people have.

Apple. Apple’s Legacy Contact lets you name someone, or more than one someone, to request access to the data in your Apple Account after you die. Apple’s own support page, published in September 2026, spells out the mechanics. You generate an access key when you set it up. Your contact needs that key and your death certificate to file the request. Apple tells you plainly what they can’t reach: anything in iCloud Keychain, which means saved passwords, passkeys and payment information, plus movies, music, books and subscriptions you bought. You need a device running iOS 15.2, iPadOS 15.2 or macOS Monterey 12.1 or later, and your contact has to be at least thirteen, with the age varying by country.

Two things on that page earned a note in my own file. If you name more than one Legacy Contact, any one of them can act alone, and that includes permanently deleting everything. And Apple suggests printing the access key and keeping a copy with your estate planning papers, which is the first time a technology company has agreed with my green folder about anything.

Google. Google’s Inactive Account Manager does a related job from a different angle. You choose how long Google should wait after your account goes quiet, and you pick up to ten people to notify, each with their own slice of your data or none of it. Google’s help page explains that it watches sign-ins, recent activity, Gmail use and Android check-ins to decide whether you’re still around, and that it asks for a trusted contact’s phone number so a stranger holding a forwarded email can’t download your life.

The same page carries a line I’d put in front of anyone who keeps twenty years of photographs in Google Photos. Set up no plan, and Google reserves the right to delete an inactive account along with its data, once you’ve been inactive across Google for at least two years.

Two years of silence, and the pictures are a company’s to delete.

Other services have their own versions, under their own names, and they change the names. Rather than print a list that’s wrong by the time you read it, do this: open each account you’d hate to lose, look in the settings for anything about legacy, memorialization, inactivity or a trusted contact, and use it. Then write down that you did, and when.

The phone is the master key

Here’s the thing people miss while they’re worrying about their email.

Your phone is not one of your accounts. It’s the key to the rest of them. The bank texts a code to it. The brokerage app lives on it. If you use an authenticator app, those six-digit codes may live only on that handset, or they may sync to an account or have a recovery process. It depends on the product and how you set it up.

Either way, a locked phone with an unknown passcode can stop a competent, authorized agent cold. I’ve watched it happen to a woman in our township whose husband had done everything else right.

So where the passcode is kept goes on your list. Not the sticky note. The list.

And if you use an authenticator app, go into it this week and check which kind yours is. Record the recovery method, never a live code. Then ask each bank and brokerage what an authorized agent may use to get in, because that answer is theirs to give, not mine.

Password managers, and the envelope question

CISA, the federal cybersecurity agency, tells people to use a password manager rather than write passwords down. I agree, and security is only half my reason. A manager is the one place where a death plan can be built into the lock itself.

A lot of them offer some kind of emergency or inherited access, where a person you name can request entry and gets it after a waiting period if you don’t refuse. That documented process is the method I’d use first. Read how yours works, specifically. How long the wait is, whether the person needs their own account, and what happens to the manager itself if the subscription lapses after you’re gone.

Which leaves the question everybody asks me: what about the things the manager can’t hand over, like the passcode to the phone the manager lives on?

Not in your will. I’m not going to make a claim about how public a will is in your state, because that varies and I’d be guessing. The reason is simpler and it applies everywhere. A will is a document you can only change by signing it again in front of witnesses. A password is a thing you change in March when the bank makes you. Don’t put a moving part inside a document built not to move.

What Dale and I did: we each named the other for emergency access in the manager, and Jess as the backup. The master password is not written anywhere. The only paper is a sealed, dated envelope holding our two phone passcodes, because emergency access can’t reach those. It sits in a locked box, not loose in the green file. Two people may open it, Jess and the one of us still living, and the note on the front says so.

The front also says, in Dale’s block capitals, that the envelope gives nobody permission to sign in as us. It’s there so an authorized person can open a phone and find the institutions, then go through each one’s own process.

The list of accounts lives outside the envelope, where it can be updated with a pen. The envelope gets opened once a year, rewritten if anything changed, and resealed with a new date.

Is that perfect security? No. The alternative we were running before, a word and four numbers taped where the church directory lives, was not a security system at all.

Chapter 12 takes up where the originals go and who holds copies, including the key to that box.

The money and the photographs

Two categories need their own minute.

Accounts with money in them that never mail you anything. A bank with no branches. A payment app holding a balance you forgot about. A brokerage you opened on your phone in 2021. Put each one on Chapter 2’s asset map and check its beneficiary form like any other account. Then put it on the digital list as well, because finding these is the hard part. Go through twelve months of bank statements and look for transfers out to a name you don’t recognize. That’s how I found one of ours.

If you hold cryptocurrency in a wallet you control yourself, understand what that means for your family: there is no help line that can reset it. The key is the asset. Tell your lawyer you have it, before you write anything about it anywhere, and ask how they want it handled.

The photographs. Twenty-two thousand of them, in our case, which is a number I did not enjoy learning. Nobody will fight over your photos in a courtroom, and everybody wants them. A copy on a drive in the house, refreshed once a year, costs almost nothing and takes the whole question out of a company’s hands.

Same for anything that documents the family: the recipes, the scanned letters, the video of your father at the kitchen table that exists in exactly one place.

And the other direction. If there are things you want gone, say so, in writing, in the letter of instruction rather than in the will. You may not get it honored. You’ll get a lot closer than by saying nothing. One sentence is enough.

Your digital list

One page, or two. It goes with the plan. Dale’s version took him fifty minutes, most of it spent discovering what the shop’s website renewal was actually charging him.

  • Devices. Each phone, tablet and computer. Who uses it, and where the passcode is kept. Write the location, not the number.
  • Email. Every address, including the one from the old provider that still receives statements. Mark which one is used to reset the others, because that one is the keystone.
  • The switches you’ve set. Apple Legacy Contact, Google Inactive Account Manager, and anything similar elsewhere. Name the person and the date you set it up. Note where the Apple access key is.
  • Money online. Branchless banks, payment apps, brokerages, the business’s merchant account, anything with a stored card. Name the institution, give four digits of the account and no more, and cross-reference the asset map.
  • Subscriptions and autopay. What would keep billing a dead man’s card, and what breaks if it stops. The domain name for the business website belongs here.
  • Photos and files. Where they are, whether there’s a copy outside the cloud, and who should end up with them.
  • Social accounts. For each: delete, memorialize, or leave alone. Three words, your choice, in your handwriting.
  • The delete list. Anything you’d rather nobody read. No explanation required.
  • Password manager. Which one, who has emergency access, and how long their waiting period is.

Date it at the bottom. Initial it. Put the date on next March’s review with everything else.

And when you see the lawyer, ask for two specific things: language in your will giving consent to disclosure of the content of your electronic communications, and matching language in your financial POA so your agent can act while you’re alive. Chapter 7 told you to ask for it. This is what you’re asking for, and it’s a paragraph, not an hour.

Dale rewrote the sticky note as line two of our list that same evening. Then he went out to the garage, came back with a putty knife, and scraped the old one off the cabinet door, because the adhesive had gone hard and the thing had earned it.

Take the trash bag and go look inside your own cabinet doors. You’ll find one.

Chapter 10: Second Marriages, Stepchildren, Singles and Other Plans That Need Extra Care

Kevin called on a Tuesday in March of 2024, the same month Dale and I were sorting passwords out of kitchen cabinets. Nine-fifteen at night, which for Kevin means he’s just remembered something he meant to do in January.

“Quick question,” he said, which from Kevin means forty minutes. “Linda and I did one of those online wills. Everything to each other. Arizona’s one of those community property states, right? So that’s fine?”

Linda is Kevin’s second wife; they married in 2019. She has two grown daughters from her first marriage. Kevin has Tyler, nineteen that spring, from his. I could hear a basketball game on low in the background, and I could hear him waiting for me to say yes.

“It’s fine,” I told him, “for whoever dies second.”

He was quiet long enough that I knew he hadn’t thought about the second part.

What “everything to each other” actually promises

Here’s the mechanism, plainly. If Kevin dies first, his will leaves everything to Linda. Linda is now alive, in charge of everything that was Kevin’s, with her own will, which she can rewrite the next morning if she wants to. She has no legal obligation to leave Tyler a dime. Neither does the reverse protect her daughters if she goes first. “Everything to each other” is really “everything to whoever outlives the other one, and then whatever that person decides.”

A surviving spouse may intend to provide for stepchildren, but a plan built on “I trust her to take care of my son” is built on hope, and hope is not one of this book’s five pieces of paper.

What people use instead, when they want Tyler’s share protected no matter what Linda does afterward:

  • A trust that supports the survivor for their life, with whatever’s left going to a named split between both sides of the family when the survivor dies. A lawyer can draft a trust that limits what the survivor may redirect and names the remainder beneficiaries. How much protection it actually gives depends on its terms and on which assets end up inside it.
  • Beneficiary forms split at the account level instead of the will level. Subject to the plan’s rules and any spousal consent it requires, Kevin could ask whether his retirement account permits a split between Linda and Tyler.
  • Life insurance bought specifically for one side of the family. If the house and the retirement account are going to Linda, a policy naming Tyler evens the ledger without anyone having to divide the house.

All three deserve legal advice in a blended family. A lawyer can draft the trust and help coordinate the institution-issued beneficiary forms and insurance designation with the rest of the plan. Which one fits depends on things I can’t see from Kevin’s kitchen: how old Tyler is, whether Linda’s daughters are grown and independent, whether the house is titled jointly, how much there is to split in the first place. I told Kevin that on the phone. I’m telling you here. This is the chapter where I say, more than anywhere else in this book, don’t do it yourself.

Stepchildren are not heirs unless you say so

Tyler calls Linda “Linda,” not “Mom,” and that’s their business. But here’s what the law doesn’t care about: affection. A will can provide for stepchildren the same as it can provide for friends and charities, people intestacy would otherwise skip entirely. Without that will, state law decides who inherits, and state law generally follows blood and marriage, not the dinner table. I’ve said this sentence in earlier chapters about other people: a will can do what intestacy won’t. In a blended household it’s the sentence that matters most, because the people intestacy is most likely to skip are the ones sitting at your table every night.

State intestacy rules vary, but do not assume a stepchild will inherit by default. If you want a stepchild to receive property, name them in a properly signed will and coordinate any beneficiary forms. Don’t rely on a family label to carry them in. Give your lawyer each person’s full name and relationship, and ask how the will should define the beneficiary class.

Community property and spousal rights don’t bend for a second marriage

I mentioned, back in Chapter 2, that nine states plus three opt-in states treat most of what a married couple earns during the marriage as owned by both of them equally, regardless of whose name is on the account. Arizona is one of the nine. That rule doesn’t know or care that it’s Kevin’s second marriage. It applies the same as it would to a couple married sixty years.

Separate property states have their own version: an elective share, letting a surviving spouse claim a portion of the estate even if the will tries to leave them out. Traditionally that figure runs around a third in states that use it, though the fraction and what it’s measured against vary, and your state’s number may be different. A will written to disinherit a current spouse in favor of children from a first marriage can run straight into that statute and lose.

None of this is something you plan around by writing clever language at your kitchen table. If Kevin wanted Tyler to get the bulk of a specific account and Linda to get something else specific, that has to be built by someone who knows which of those rules apply in Arizona, to his accounts, in his situation. I told him to bring the question to a lawyer there, not to guess from what worked for Dale and me in Ohio.

One more piece, already familiar to you from Chapter 3: some retirement plans require the current spouse be named beneficiary unless that spouse signs a specific, witnessed consent to name someone else. A man who wants his 401(k) split between his second wife and his son from his first marriage cannot simply write that on the beneficiary card and assume it holds. If Kevin’s plan requires the current spouse to be beneficiary, Linda would need to sign the plan’s properly witnessed consent before any share could go to Tyler. Kevin should ask the plan administrator which rule and form apply. Skip that step and the form may default right back to her for the whole account, no matter what anyone intended.

Unmarried and living together

A man in our township, whose name I won’t use because he’d rather I didn’t, lived with a woman for nineteen years. Never married. When he was hospitalized with a stroke, she sat in a waiting room while his sister, who he’d spoken to maybe four times in a decade, made the decisions. An unmarried partner may have no inheritance rights under your state’s default rules, and may be excluded from medical decisions unless you name them in a health care power of attorney. Check your state law with a lawyer before relying on any default. Not because anyone intends it. Because the forms ask about marriage, not about love or nineteen years of grocery lists.

If you are unmarried and living with someone you want provided for, the paperwork matters more than it would for a married couple, not less. Don’t assume married-spouse defaults protect your partner. Ask a lawyer what status and default rights your state recognizes, then name the partner explicitly wherever it’s needed. In the will. On the health care power of attorney from Chapter 8. As a beneficiary on the accounts where that matters. Say it in writing, in every place it needs saying.

Single, with no children

Bev was this chapter, before she was Chapter 3’s cautionary tale about a payable-on-death account. Widowed, no children, choosing who got what without a spouse’s rights or a child’s expectations to weigh against. She picked me. Someone else might pick a niece, a church, a friend from forty years back, a hospital that treated them well once.

If that’s your situation, the work isn’t harder, just different. Choose your people and name them specifically, because without a spouse or children, state intestacy law keeps looking, through parents, then siblings, then more and more distant relatives, until it finds someone, and the person it finds may not be who you’d have picked. In rare cases with no relatives at all, the property can end up belonging to the state. Name a health care agent even though there’s no assumed spouse standing by to take the job. If you want to leave something to a cause rather than a person, say so by name, with the organization’s full legal name if you can find it. “The hospital” or “the shelter” isn’t specific enough for a form, let alone a will.

A child or heir with money trouble, or a disability

This is lawyer territory. If you’re planning to leave money to someone who receives needs-based government benefits, a direct inheritance may affect those benefits. SSA says that both a trust’s terms and its payments can affect SSI and Medicaid, so consult a lawyer who handles benefits planning before you name this person on a will, trust, or beneficiary form. The same caution applies to an heir with a gambling problem or an addiction a family is actively managing: the lawyer can build in a trustee’s discretion instead of handing over a lump sum.

If Medicaid and nursing home costs are part of what you’re worried about for yourself, that’s a longer conversation than this book can carry. One clause: see an elder law attorney, and start before a crisis, not during one.

Divorce and separation

This book is about your own plan and not about dividing up a marriage. If you’re divorced or separating, update everything: the will, every beneficiary form, both powers of attorney, the health care directive. Do not rely on an automatic-revocation rule. Ask a lawyer what your state does, then change every document and institution-issued form yourself. For beneficiary forms, use the five-step audit in Chapter 3; the money side of divorce belongs in Gray Divorce After 50. This chapter only asks you to touch every document on your list the week the papers are final, not the week you remember to.

The test: run your plan through four deaths that haven’t happened yet

Here’s the tool. It isn’t legal advice; it’s a way to catch the gap before a lawyer has to.

Take your current plan, or your draft of one, and walk it through four scenarios, writing down who ends up with what in each:

  1. You die first. Who gets what, right now, under what you’ve signed or what you’re about to sign?
  2. Your spouse dies first, then remarries. If your spouse later marries someone new, does your plan still reach your children, or does it now depend entirely on your spouse’s new will?
  3. You and your spouse die in the same accident. Does the plan address who is treated as surviving whom, or does it leave the result to state law?
  4. A child or stepchild dies before you do. Does their share pass to their own children, or back to their siblings? If the document doesn’t answer, which residue, lapse, anti-lapse or intestacy rule would govern, and is that the result you want? Ask your lawyer.

Kevin and Linda ran this after their lawyer visit that spring.
