Scenario two was the one that stopped them cold: their online will said nothing about what happened if the surviving spouse remarried, because the template didn’t ask. They added a clause. It cost them one more conversation with the lawyer and, Kevin told me, considerably more than the online service had, though I’m not going to put a number on either one.

Write your four answers down. If any of them surprises you, that’s the one to bring to Chapter 11.

I told Kevin, before we hung up that night, that “everything to each other” wasn’t wrong. It just wasn’t finished. He laughed and said that described most of what he’d done at twenty-six, too.

Tyler doesn’t know any of this happened. That’s probably right, for now. But the conversation happened before anyone signed anything, which is the only part of this chapter I’d insist on for every blended family, married five years or forty: say out loud, before you sign, who you’re trying to protect. The document can’t do that part. Only you can.

Chapter 11: Hiring and Briefing an Estate Lawyer (and When You Can Do It Yourself)

Sam’s office sits above the hardware store, up a flight of stairs with a rubber runner worn pale in the middle. The waiting room has four chairs, a coffee table and a farm magazine from 2019 that I have now read twice.

We had the two-fifteen on a Tuesday in April of 2024. I brought the green accordion file with both hands, the way you carry a casserole.

Sam’s clock runs in tenths of an hour. Six minutes to a tenth, and a tenth is the smallest thing he can write down, which means a two-minute phone call costs six minutes and a question you could have answered yourself costs six minutes.

He had told me on the phone to block out two hours.

It took fifty-two minutes.

Not because Sam is fast. Because every question he asked that afternoon, I already had on paper in front of me. What do you own. In what state. Titled how. Who’s named on the retirement accounts. Who’s your agent if you can’t sign. Who’s the backup. The trust question took about the four minutes Chapter 6 already described, and it appeared on the bill as one six-minute unit, because one unit is the smallest thing on his sheet.

I am not claiming we saved a specific amount of money. I don’t know what the two-hour version would have cost, because we never bought it. What I can tell you is that sixty-eight minutes of a lawyer’s attention did not get spent on me reciting the name of our credit union.

What a lawyer is actually for, and what they’re not

The American Bar Association has a page called “The Lawyer’s Role,” and it is blunter about do-it-yourself kits than I expected. It says it’s easy to be lured by advertising that promises you can save time and money drafting your own will or trust from a website, retail software or a fill-in-the-blank kit. It says it’s unlikely those alternatives will produce a plan that accomplishes everything you want. Its specific complaint is worth repeating, because it isn’t about typing. A canned form, the ABA says, can’t assure you that the form is correct, that assets passing outside your will are properly handled, that state law nuances are accounted for, or that the relevant tax, legal and personal issues are addressed.

Now the fair caveat, which I’d want if I were you. That page is published by an association of lawyers, and it is telling you to hire a lawyer. Read it knowing that.

But look at the four things on its list again and notice that three of them are the exact problems this book has spent ten chapters on. Assets passing outside the will is Chapter 3, and it’s the one most people get wrong. State nuance is every other paragraph. “Relevant personal issues” is Chapter 10’s whole subject.

So here is my honest split, and it isn’t the ABA’s and it isn’t the kit sellers’.

There is one part of this plan I would do myself without a second thought, and the National Institute on Aging agrees: the advance directives. Chapter 8 quoted the NIA on that, and gave you the free places to get your state’s forms. Hand your lawyer a copy if you have one. Dale and I filled ours in at the kitchen table in March, and Sam read them in about five minutes and said they were fine.

The will, the financial power of attorney and anything involving a trust, I would not do myself. Chapter 4 already told you where I’d put the money, and it’s the will. Partly that’s the drafting. Mostly it’s the signing, because an unwitnessed or badly witnessed will can fail at exactly the moment nobody can fix it.

And then there’s a list of situations where I wouldn’t just hire a lawyer, I’d hire one before I filled in a single beneficiary form.

A second marriage, or stepchildren, or anybody’s children from before. Minor children, or any child young enough to need the money held. Real estate in a second state. A business, including a small business like Dale’s. An heir who receives needs-based benefits, or one who can’t be handed a lump sum. Anybody you intend to leave out. And any family where you can already name the person who will be unhappy and the sibling they’ll call about it.

Those are each a single line here because each one has its own chapter, and I’m not going to re-argue them. What matters is that you recognize your own situation on that list and stop reading advertisements.

If money is the thing standing in the way

It usually is, and nobody says so out loud.

The NIA, writing about the health care side, points people who need help with planning to their local Area Agency on Aging, and names three other routes: state legal aid offices, state bar associations, and local nonprofit agencies, foundations and social service agencies. The Eldercare Locator number is in Chapter 8. Those referral routes are worth a phone call before you decide a plan is out of reach, and a phone call is the whole cost of finding out.

The other free resource is one this book has leaned on all the way through: state court self-help websites. California’s is the one I’ve quoted, because it’s unusually good and it’s public, and I used its guardianship pages in Chapter 5 and its probate pages in Chapter 6. Find out whether your own state courts publish something like it. They won’t give you advice, and they won’t draft anything, but they will often tell you plainly what your state requires, which is half of what you’re afraid of not knowing.

What I would not do is let the cost question push you toward signing nothing.

I can’t tell you which document is cheapest or which order is safe, because there is no universal answer and no source worth trusting that claims one. What I can tell you is where the free route is. If your state publishes an advance-directive form and your situation is the ordinary kind Chapter 8 described, fill that one in now. The NIA says you don’t need a lawyer for it, and the forms come from your Attorney General’s office or your Area Agency on Aging at no cost. Do that part tonight and it’s done.

For everything else, make the order somebody else’s job. Ask legal aid, or the first estate lawyer you get on the phone, what has to be drafted first given your particular risks, what each stage costs, and what can safely wait a year. That is a fair question and a short one. Marlene asked a version of it after the seminar and got her answer before she spent anything.

How I’d go looking

Ask your people first. The ABA’s own advice, after all the warnings about kits, is that the most important thing is to choose an attorney you have confidence in, through recommendations from friends or from your other professional advisors. That second half is the one people skip. If you have an accountant, ask them. They watch the aftermath of other people’s estate plans and they have opinions they’ll share if asked directly.

Then check the qualifications, and know what you’re looking at. The ABA explains that not every state requires or allows lawyers to designate a specialty, which in law as in medicine is generally called board certification. Its own Committee on Specialization keeps information on those programs, including state bar programs and programs the ABA has approved. So “board certified in estate planning” means something real in a state that has such a program and means nothing at all in a state that doesn’t. Ask which yours is.

Membership signals are softer but not worthless. The ABA says that belonging to certain bar associations or estate planning organizations often indicates dedication to the field. It gives one example by name. Becoming a fellow of the American College of Trust and Estate Counsel, ACTEC, generally indicates extensive experience in estate planning as well as substantial service to the profession. It’s a signal, not a requirement. Sam is not a fellow of anything, as far as I know. He has sat across a desk from several hundred families in this county and he returns phone calls.

One filter of my own. I want a lawyer who does this work most weeks, not one who does real estate closings and will “take a look at a will for you.” The difference shows up in the questions they ask in the first ten minutes. A lawyer who does this often asks how things are titled before asking what they’re worth.

Fees, and why you won’t find numbers in this chapter

I’m not going to print a dollar range for estate planning work, and I want to tell you why rather than just leave the gap.

There is no official source for it. Not the IRS, not the ABA, not a state court. Every figure I could find came from a company with a reason to publish it, and fees move with your state, your county, your facts and the hour of that lawyer’s life you happen to catch. If I printed a range, you’d carry it into Sam’s office as an expectation, and you’d either feel cheated or overpay with confidence. Both are worse than walking in and asking.

So ask, directly, in the first conversation. The ABA says to be sure to ask your attorney about legal fees, and to see that they’re settled to your satisfaction in the written agreement between you and the attorney. That agreement is often called the engagement letter. The ABA adds that most states don’t require one, and that you probably should have one anyway. Ask for it in writing.

What to pin down, in the same breath as the number: whether it’s a flat fee for the package or billed by the hour, and exactly what’s inside it. Does it include the deed, if a deed has to change? Does it include funding a trust, if you’re getting one, or does that come later at an hourly rate? Does it include one round of revisions after you read the draft? Does it include the signing appointment and the witnesses? And what does a change cost in three years when a grandchild arrives?

The ABA also mentions that ACTEC’s website publishes model engagement letters for a range of estate planning matters, which is a strange and useful thing to know. You can read what a thorough one looks like before you sign yours.

The briefing packet

This is the part that turns a two-hour meeting into a fifty-two-minute one, and it’s almost entirely work you’ve already done.

The ABA’s preparation advice is to organize your information on assets, liabilities and title arrangements, and to think about how you feel about providing for various family members. It adds that most lawyers in this area have questionnaires to help. It also says to bring copies of the important documents: previous wills or trusts, powers of attorney, life insurance policies, employment benefits, prenuptial agreements and divorce decrees.

Here’s that list in the form I actually walked in with. Clip it together. Bring copies, keep your originals.

  • The asset map from Chapter 2. Every line, with the exact title words and the road each item travels. Mine ran to twenty-three lines and three of them still said ASK.
  • The beneficiary audit from Chapter 3, including the forms you already fixed and the dates you fixed them. This is the sheet that stops a lawyer from designing around a mistake you’ve corrected, or missing one you haven’t.
  • The will decision sheet from Chapter 4. Executor and backup, the residue in percentages, backup takers, the short list of specific gifts, and your sentence about anyone you mean to leave out. That last line is for the lawyer’s eyes, not the will’s.
  • The guardian pages from Chapter 5, if you have children at home, with the date you asked the person.
  • The agent questions from Chapter 7 and the completed health care directives from Chapter 8, plus the name and phone number of each agent and backup.
  • The digital list from Chapter 9, or at least the two paragraph requests it told you to make.
  • Debts and obligations. Mortgage, loans, anything you’ve co-signed, anything the business owes.
  • The old paperwork. Prior wills and trusts, existing powers of attorney, insurance policies including the group coverage from work, your employer’s benefits summary, any prenuptial agreement, any divorce decree, and the deed to anything you own.
  • One page of questions, which is the next section.

Mine fit in the green file with room over. Sam put the asset map on top of the pile and worked from it the whole hour. When he wrote the will he used my percentages and my backup takers almost word for word. Judgment was the thing I’d brought. Drafting was the thing I’d hired.

Twelve questions for the first meeting

Write these on one sheet and take it in. Cross off the ones that get answered before you ask.

  1. How much of your practice is wills, trusts and estates?
  2. Is specialty certification available in this state, and are you certified?
  3. Looking at my asset map, what passes outside the will, and does anything need to change?
  4. Given these facts, do I need a trust, and what would it do that my will and powers of attorney wouldn’t?
  5. What does my state require for the signing of each document, and who arranges the witnesses?
  6. Is the fee flat or hourly, what’s included, and will I get an engagement letter?
  7. What’s not included, and what does it cost?
  8. Who holds the originals, and what do I take home that day?
  9. What happens to this plan if we move to another state?
  10. What should I do myself and not pay you for?
  11. Who do I call if you retire, and what happens to my file?
  12. What would you do differently if these were your facts?

That last one has never failed me. The answer tells you whether the person across the desk is selling a document or thinking about your family, and you can hear the difference in the first six words.

Number eleven I learned from Helen, who lost the doctor she’d had for nineteen years and discovered in Chapter 7 what that cost her.

Signing day

The second Thursday in May 2024, late afternoon, because Dale had a service call in Waverly that morning.

Sam’s conference room has a window unit that rattles. Two people from his office came in to witness, and a woman from the title company downstairs came up with her notary stamp and a sleeve of stickers. Sam told us how many witnesses the signing needed and in what order it all had to happen. That’s exactly the kind of thing that varies state to state. Take your own state’s answer from your own lawyer, not from my kitchen.

Then we read every page.

All of it, with Sam waiting. He expected it. I found one thing: my middle name was misspelled on page one of the financial document, written the way people assume instead of the way it is. It took four minutes to fix and reprint. Had I skimmed, some bank clerk in 2031 would have been the one to find it, with Dale sitting across the desk unable to pay his own electric bill.

Dale signed first. He wrote his name the way he writes it on invoices, and when he finished the will he set the pen down and said, “Fourteen minutes.” He’d been timing it.

We left with a folder of copies and the documents Sam recommended we keep in our own hands. Where the originals ended up, and who got which copy, is Chapter 12, and it is not a small question.

What I remember from the stairs on the way down is how ordinary it felt. No weight lifted, no moment. A rattling window unit, a stranger’s notary stamp, a woman I’d known since the fourth grade asking me to initial page six.

Six months earlier, Jess had asked me where mine was, and I’d had nothing to say.

Call one office this week and ask for a first appointment. Then start filling the packet, because the appointment is the easy half.

Chapter 12: Keep It Where They’ll Find It, and Look at It Every March

The first Saturday in March of 2025, Dale carried the green accordion file to the kitchen table and set it down the way he sets down a part he has already decided is bad.

Nine months earlier we had signed everything in Sam’s conference room with the window unit rattling. I had put a note on the December calendar page that said MARCH, FILE, because I knew that otherwise we would do it in July, or we would do it never.

It took forty minutes.

Thirty-eight of those minutes were me reading things out loud and Dale saying “still right” with a coffee cup in his hand. Executor, still right. Agents, still right. Jess’s address, still right. Directives, unchanged, both of us in the same health we were in last spring.

Then we got to the credit union line on the asset map and it had gone wrong without anybody doing anything wrong.

In October of 2024 I had moved money out of our credit union savings into a fifteen-month certificate, because the rate was better and I am my mother’s daughter. New account. New number. New signature card. Nobody at the counter asked me about a beneficiary, and it did not occur to me to ask them, because in my head that money was still the account I had written down in January with POD: Jess beside it in pencil.

It wasn’t. The savings account still had Jess on it and about forty dollars in it. The certificate had the money and nobody named.

Nothing terrible had happened. Notice that. Our will sends that money to the same place the POD designation would have, so nothing was waiting to detonate.

What it was is a road change we never chose. Chapter 2 gave you the four roads. In five minutes at a counter I had moved most of our cash off the beneficiary-form road and onto the will’s road. That road ordinarily becomes probate property and follows whatever court or qualifying small-estate process state law provides. I had done it while believing the opposite.

That is what a yearly review is actually for. Not for the dramatic thing. For the thing that moved while you weren’t looking.

I fixed it the following Tuesday at the branch. One signature card, one copy to bring home, two lines corrected on the asset map in pen. Dale drew a small star next to the new line, which is his filing system.

Where the originals live

There is one rule here and it holds everywhere. No original should be somewhere your authorized person cannot reach when it is needed.

Not your locked desk whose key is on your keyring. Not a box in the attic nobody else knows about. Not, and I say this because I have seen it, inside a hollowed-out book, which was a real thing a real man in this county did with a will.

Beyond that rule, there are three ordinary homes for original documents, and the right one depends on answers you have to go get.

Your lawyer’s office. Many firms will hold original wills in a vault. If yours does, ask what happens to your file if that lawyer retires or the firm closes, which is question eleven from Chapter 11 and the one people skip because it feels rude. Get the answer in writing if you can, and write down the firm’s phone number somewhere your family will find it.

A fireproof box at home. The advantage is that your agent can get a document into a bank on a Tuesday morning without an appointment. Make sure a second person knows where the box is and how to open it, and that your agent is one of them.

A safe deposit box. Before you use one, ask the bank in writing. Who can enter while you are alive but unable to act. Who can enter after death. What authority and which documents each of those people needs. Whether a renter or an agent may remove a document. How the lease and state law affect those answers. Death-only access is not enough; your financial agent may need the original while you are still living. Banks have their own procedures and state rules differ, and the answer also depends on how the box is rented and whose name is on it. If timely access is uncertain, keep that original elsewhere. I am not going to tell you what your bank will say. I am telling you to find out before, rather than have your daughter find out after.

Here is what we did, so you have one concrete version to argue with. Sam keeps the original will in his vault, and we hold a copy stamped as a copy, with a sheet clipped to it saying where the original sits and who to call. The financial powers of attorney we keep ourselves, in a fireproof box on the floor of the hall closet. Chapter 7 is the whole reason: an agent frequently has to physically produce that document, and one your agent can’t reach on the worst morning of the year isn’t working for you. The health care directives went out to the people on Chapter 8’s copies list, and the file copy lives in the green accordion file with everything else.

One more thing worth asking your own lawyer, since I can’t answer it for you: whether your state offers any official place to deposit a will for safekeeping, and whether they would recommend it in your situation. Mine is an Ohio question and Ohio law is not mine to state.

Who gets a copy, and who just gets told

Copies are cheap. Confusion is not.

Your financial agent needs the signed document in hand, or needs to know exactly where it is and to be able to get there without you. Give your successor agent the same information. Clip Chapter 7’s first-week sheet to the copy, because the document says they may act and the sheet says what to actually do on day one.

Your health care proxy, your alternate and your doctor are already handled by the copies list in Chapter 8, and I’m not going to repeat it here. Make sure that list and this one were done in the same month, so you don’t have a 2024 proxy holding a 2026 directive.

Your executor needs to know where the will is. That’s it. They don’t need to hold an original, and my own preference, which is a preference and not a rule, is that they shouldn’t, because documents in circulation get superseded and the superseded one is the one that turns up. Tell them the location and the lawyer’s name. Tell them out loud, with a date, the way Chapter 4 told you to ask them in the first place.

And then one person who is not any of the above should know that the green file exists and which drawer it is in. In our house that’s Jess. She has never read a page of it. She could put her hand on it in the dark.

The letter of instruction

A letter of instruction is practical guidance, not a legal document. It cannot transfer the dog or the dishes, change a beneficiary, appoint an agent, or authorize account access. Put legally operative choices in the proper signed document; use this letter for locations, contacts, routines, and preferences.

What it is good for is the page that answers the questions your will is too formal to answer and your family will be asking in the first week, when they are not at their most resourceful.

Mine is two sides of one sheet, and it says: where the original will is and Sam’s number. Where the asset map lives and that the account numbers on it are the last four digits only, by design. That the house insurance renews in August and the agent’s name is on the policy in the file. That the dog is thirteen and hates the groomer on Fourth Street, and that Jess has agreed to care for the dog; the lawyer confirmed where that arrangement belongs in the signed plan. That the photographs in the hall closet are the only ones I care about and the digital copies from Chapter 9 are on the drive in the same closet. That I would like the good dishes used rather than divided. That Marlene across the road should be called early, because she will know who else to call, and that is a job somebody has to do.

None of that is enforceable. All of it saves somebody an afternoon.

Write yours in your own voice, date it, and rewrite it when it stops being true. It is also the right place for the deletion wishes from Chapter 9, and the wrong place for anything that belongs in the will.

When to look at it

Twice, in two different ways.

The calendar way is once a year. The National Institute on Aging says to treat your advance directives as living documents, review them at least once each year, and update them after a major life event, naming retirement, a move out of state, or a significant change in your health. That’s their advice about the medical papers specifically, and I have borrowed the rhythm for the whole file, because once I have the file open anyway, checking six more lines costs me nothing.

The American Bar Association adds a separate clock for one item. It says your insurance coverage should be reviewed at least every two or three years, to confirm the policy is performing as intended, the company remains in solid financial position, and the ownership and beneficiary designations still match your wishes. That last clause is the one that catches people. A policy can be fine and still be pointed at the wrong person.

The second way isn’t a calendar at all. It’s a list of things that, when they happen, mean you open the file that week instead of waiting for March.

Somebody named in any document dies. Somebody named gets married or divorced, including you. A child or grandchild arrives. You move to another state. What you own changes substantially, in either direction. Someone’s health or capacity changes, including the agent you picked for exactly this reason. Someone named comes into money trouble, or starts relying on needs-based benefits, which sends you back to Chapter 10 and then to a lawyer.

And the quiet one: a law or a figure changes. The federal exclusion number I gave you in Chapter 1 came with a year attached for a reason, and state rules move too. You don’t have to track legislation. You have to reread the sources named in Chapter 1 once a year, on the same Saturday, and notice whether the number has a different year on it now.

Changing things without breaking them

What you change depends on which road the thing travels, which is why Chapter 2 came first.

Beneficiary forms are changed at the institution, never in the will, and the change isn’t done until the confirmation is in your hand. Chapter 3 gave you the five steps and the audit sheet. Rerun that sheet every March. My credit union certificate is the reason I say so in this tone.

The will is a lawyer visit. A codicil is still available to you, under the signing rules Chapter 4 laid out and with the ABA’s warning about ambiguity between the two documents. I told you there where I come down, and I won’t re-argue it. Ask your lawyer to quote both ways and to say which they’d do with your facts.

Titles and deeds are their own job. Chapter 6 told you to get a written answer from the institution and the lawyer before moving an account into a trust, and the same question applies to any retitling at all, including the cheerful kind where someone adds a child’s name to make things easier. Ask it before the signature card, not after.

Powers of attorney travel better than people expect. The ABA says a power of attorney that was valid when you signed it generally remains valid after you move, and then says to update it anyway as part of an overall review. Both halves of that are true at once. If you own real property in a second state, the ABA says to check with an attorney that your document covers it.

Advance directives are the exception to “it probably still works.” The NIA says that if you spend a lot of time in more than one state, consider preparing the form for each state and keeping a copy in each place. Chapter 8 gave you the NIA’s rules for retiring an old version, and gave you the revocation steps that go with them. Do both. A new directive is not in force in any practical sense while last year’s copy is still sitting in somebody’s filing cabinet looking valid.

What you tell the family, and what you don’t

I have an opinion here and it isn’t universal.

Tell your grown children the structure. Do not tell them the balances.

The structure is: who holds which job, where the file is, who to call first, that there is a will and a lawyer and where. That information is useful to them, costs you nothing, and prevents the specific kind of grief where somebody spends the week after a funeral searching a house. We told Jess all of it at a Sunday supper, and she asked two questions.

The balances are a different thing. They change every year, they invite arithmetic, and the arithmetic is almost always done by somebody who is not in the room. Numbers also go stale in a way that jobs don’t. What you tell a thirty-two-year-old about your retirement account in 2026 will be wrong by 2029 and remembered as a promise.

If a particular choice in your plan is going to surprise somebody, that is a separate conversation and you should have it while you can be asked follow-up questions. Chapter 1 made the case for that and I’m not making it twice. Just don’t confuse “I explained my reasoning” with “I read them the statements.”

The March review checklist

One page. Put it in the front pocket, in front of everything, so it’s the first thing your hand touches.

  1. Read last year’s date on the inside flap. Write down what’s happened since.
  2. Will: still names the right executor, backup, residue split and backup takers. Any name changed, moved, died or married.
  3. Guardian nomination, if you have children at home: person still willing, still in the right place, backup still valid.
  4. Financial power of attorney: agent and successors still right, still told, still reachable. Phone numbers current.
  5. Health care directive and proxy: reviewed per Chapter 8’s list. Copies in the right six places. Old versions dated and filed.
  6. Beneficiary audit from Chapter 3, rerun line by line against this year’s statements. Every account for which the institution offers a beneficiary designation, including eligible accounts opened since last March; mark the rest N/A and confirm their road.
  7. Any new account, new deed, new vehicle, new policy, new online-only anything. Add to the asset map with its road.
  8. Access test on every original: name the person who would need each document, while you are living and after, and confirm they could reach it that week. Re-ask the bank’s safe-deposit questions if anything about the box or the lease has changed.
  9. Insurance, on the ABA’s two-to-three-year clock: performing as intended, company solid, ownership and beneficiaries still right.
  10. Digital list from Chapter 9: online-tool settings still set, access key still where the note says, password envelope opened, rewritten if needed, resealed with today’s date.
  11. Letter of instruction: still true.
  12. The sources from Chapter 1: do this year’s figures have this year on them.
  13. Date the inside flap before the file goes back in the drawer.

And one page that is not a checklist, which we call the card. One side of one index card, in the front pocket and in a sealed envelope that Jess has. On it: our two names. Sam’s name and number. Where the original will is. Where the fireproof box is and how to open it. Who the agents are, for money and for medical. Where the asset map is. And one instruction at the bottom, “start with the asset map, not the house.” That card is the first thing anybody should read and the only thing they need to find.

What a review is really measuring

Forty minutes, once a year, and the only thing we found was a certificate of deposit I’d opened myself five months earlier.

That’s the honest advertisement for this chapter. Not a catastrophe averted. A small, invisible drift corrected before it had eleven years to sit there, which is how long Aunt Bev’s savings account named a man who had been dead since 2011.

Bev didn’t do anything careless. She did one sensible thing in 2009 and then never opened the drawer again, and the drawer is where the damage happens.

So: put MARCH on a calendar page now, while the book is open. Then write today’s date on the inside flap of whatever folder you’ve got, even if the folder is still mostly empty, because next March you will want to know exactly how far along you were when you wrote it.

“Where’s Yours?” Again

Christmas afternoon 2025, after the plates were cleared and before anybody started hunting for a coat, I handed Jess an envelope.

Business size, her name on the front in pen. I had started to write something above her name, thought better of it, and threw that first envelope away.

She knew what was in it. We’d talked about the card in March, when she came down for a weekend and found Dale and me at the table with the green accordion file open between us. One index card, both sides used, everything Chapter 12 told you to put on it.

She read it standing up, which is how she reads everything.

Then she put it in her purse.

I had to go stand at the sink for a minute over that. For two years I moved my mother’s health care power of attorney from one handbag to the next and could not have told you why I bothered. Chapter 8 is what came of that habit, at two in the morning, behind a curtain. I never told Jess about the carrying part. She did it anyway.

Owen is four. He spent the afternoon running a fire truck along the baseboard behind the tree, and at one point he came over and asked what was in the envelope, and Jess told him “Grandma’s phone numbers,” which is true enough for four.

Marlene made the call

The Sunday after Christmas, Marlene came across the road with a coffee cake in a foil pan and cut herself a piece before her coat was off. She’s done that since the spring we moved in.

She had an appointment card in her cardigan pocket. Sam’s office, the second Tuesday in January, ten in the morning. On the back, in her own handwriting: will, POA, health care. The three she told me on the phone she’d spend her money on, the week after that steakhouse lunch where the man in the good jacket said “probate” nineteen times and never once asked anybody in the room what they owned.

That lunch was February 2024. Her appointment is January 2026.

Almost two years. I’d rather give you that number straight than tidy it up, because it may be the most useful thing in these last pages. Marlene isn’t lazy and she isn’t in denial. She is seventy-two now and nothing about her situation has gotten more complicated since that lunch. What she needed was to hear the question more than once, from somebody who wasn’t selling her anything, in a kitchen, with cake on a plate. Most people are like that. I was, and I had settled three estates.

She asked me, buttoning her coat, whether she should bring anything.

The deed, her last bank statement, and the two sheets she’d filled in at my table.

Write the date down.

The order to do it in

If you’ve read this far and signed nothing, this is the paragraph to photocopy.

Make the list first (Chapter 2), because every decision after it needs it. Then the beneficiary forms on the retirement accounts, the insurance and the bank accounts, because those move the most money and can be fixed in an afternoon (Chapter 3). Then the will (Chapter 4), with the guardian nomination in it if you have children at home (Chapter 5), and the trust question answered by your own facts rather than by a free lunch (Chapter 6). Then the two powers of attorney, money and medical, which stand a better chance of mattering before any will does (Chapters 7 and 8). Then the digital list (Chapter 9). Then put it where the people who need it can reach it, and write one Saturday a year on the calendar to read it through (Chapter 12).

Chapter 10 runs alongside all of that if your family isn’t simple, and Chapter 11 is the lawyer and how to walk in with your homework already done.

One thing I’d say once more, plainly. The advance directives Dale and I filled in ourselves, on a free form, at this table. Everything else in the stack went across Sam’s desk, and I’d do it that way again. Stepchildren, minor children, property in a second state, a business, an heir who relies on needs-based benefits, anybody who will be unhappy with what you decided: that is when you pay a lawyer licensed where you live. Not because paperwork is magic. Because the questions you don’t know to ask are the ones that cost your family money.

Nothing here is finished

I wanted finished. In the fall of 2023, sitting with that probate envelope, finished was the entire goal, and it turns out not to be a thing that exists.

What Dale and I have is current. The will is current. The forms were current as of the first Saturday in March, which is when we found the certificate of deposit I’d opened myself and discovered I had moved most of our cash onto a road we hadn’t chosen. Something else will drift this year. A company will merge. A rate will change and I’ll move money again, because I am my mother’s daughter about rates. Somebody named in those papers will get older, including me.

That isn’t failure. That’s what it is to own things and still be alive. The yearly Saturday exists because the drift exists, and forty minutes a year is a cheap way to stay honest with yourself.

Dale said it better, out in the garage three weeks after we made that first list, reading it over under his good light. He said we should have done this at forty.

He’s right. We didn’t. The folder exists anyway.

The drawer

For most of the spring of 2024, the second kitchen drawer wouldn’t close.

The green accordion file had swollen past what the drawer could take: the asset map, the beneficiary confirmations, the decision sheets, the directives, a copy of the will stamped as a copy with a note clipped to it saying where the original is. I remember putting my hip against the drawer front and hearing paper fold.

So I cleared the cabinet above the phone to make room, which is how I came to be holding a sticky note with my husband’s email password on it, taped inside a cabinet door since about 2012.

The drawer closes now. It has closed since March of 2024, and I notice it every single time, which Dale finds funny and I don’t intend to stop.

That’s the whole of what I wanted, and I didn’t know it until I had it. Not a legal strategy. Not a saved dollar I can point to. A drawer that closes, in a kitchen in Chillicothe, with one index card’s worth of instructions in my daughter’s purse eighty miles north.

Find out where yours is. Then get the drawer to close.
